Two things soften this. The README tells users about the once-a-session cap. And retail-A's A5 status reply did say "This Q4 revision is uncommitted." So this is minor and arguably a deliberate trade-off. Still, the release is the cause.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-release/SKILL.md:61 (Report: no item for producing_uncommitted_changes or packaging_uncommitted_changes; "Suggest no commit in this report when you already suggested a commit this session"). awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:5023-5052 (provenance_gaps leaves out uncommitted changes) and ~5195-5203 (release report fields: datasets, dispositions, open_caveats, provenance_gaps, checkout_only_acquisitions, storage; no uncommitted changes). awb-package/assets/package-format/manifest-template.md:18 (a SHA with uncommitted changes does not fully identify the producing code). CHANGELOG.md:156 (commit suggested at most once a session in the package and release reports). Clear rules co2-B broke once: awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:50, README.md:105, awb-init/assets/workbench/README.md:56, awb-package/SKILL.md:96. Run evidence: co2-B relay agent-002.out.md:83, agent-005.out.md:42, agent-006.in.md ("No Git commit needed"), human/notes.md:42. retail-A relay agent-003.out.md (commit suggestion), agent-009.out.md (release report, no mention), project/deliveries/marketing-budget/leadership-budget/released/001/manifest.json, project git status (untracked producer, queries, review-rules.md, package-format/).
verdicts.narrowed: Only the retail-A half holds. awb-release's Report has no item for producing_uncommitted_changes or packaging_uncommitted_changes, and the `release` output does not return them. provenance_gaps excludes them by design. The Report's "suggest no commit when you already suggested one this session" cap then blocks any reminder. So a user who committed once earlier in the session can freeze a numbered release whose producing queries and package formats are only uncommitted or untracked, recorded by checksum alone, and the release report says nothing (minor). The co2-B half, repeated commit suggestions, is an agent deviation, not a release defect. The release states the once-a-session cap clearly in AGENTS.md, both READMEs and the awb-package report. The agent broke it once (the A5 offer after the A2 suggestion), and A1 and A3 restate Git status rather than suggest a commit.

consolidated.title: The 15-word headline warning still costs a decision the preview could have caught
consolidated.description: A long headline is now a warning the user can accept with a reason, but nothing counts words at the preview. retail-B's preview claimed every headline had at most 15 words. One approved headline had 16, and it came back as a separate decision at check-draft. retail-A kept the user's 16-word headline by recording an acceptance without asking, because asking about a headline the user had just written would cost a round.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: partly: #95 (issue #89) made the limit a warning that requires asking and recording the user's reason, but added no word count at the headline checkpoint.
consolidated.evidence: retail-B-07: reply 3 ('Each headline is at most 15 words'); agent-005 check-draft row 'the headline has 16 words'; reply 5 decision 1; msg 6. retail-A-18: msg 7; reply 7 ('retained verbatim'); one accepted_long_headlines entry in the release 001 manifest. Release: awb-package/SKILL.md:54.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to blame the harness and couldn't. The retail-B part comes from the release. The retail-A part is real, but it is a different problem.

retail-B (Claude agent, Codex persona):
- Reply 3 was the preview-and-wait checkpoint, which the user asked for in msg 3 and which is also the skill's default mode. It said "Each headline is at most 15 words." Headline 4 has 16 words: "Top 10% of identified customers: 64% of identified revenue, 55% of total; 13% lacks an ID." I counted it with the release's own `_words` rule. It is also in `.preview/headlines.md` line 11.
- Reply 4 repeated the same claim ("each at most 15 words") with the same headline, and the user approved it in msg 5.
- In agent-005, check-draft returned the outline row "the headline has 16 words, over the 15-word limit". Reply 5 raised it as Decision 1, and the user chose the shorter wording in msg 6.
- The agent logs for turns 003 and 004 show the preview was written with no word count at any point.
- The release explains why. SKILL.md:54 tells the agent to *say* that a headline holds at most 15 words, but gives it nothing to count with. awb_draft.py (around line 46 and in the inventory code) deliberately keeps `.preview/` out of every check. Only check-draft counts words (HEADLINE_WORDS=15, outline_problems), and it runs after the full draft. So the agent claims compliance without checking it.

Harness causes I ruled out:
- Non-interactive `claude -p` does not affect word counting.
- The Codex sandbox is not involved, because Claude was the agent in retail-B.
- Auto-approved MCP tools, the simulated home and the relay play no part.
- The persona did not front-load this headline. The agent wrote it.
- The study disclosure in the system prompt and the friction-log note say nothing about headlines or saving rounds.
- A real user approving headlines would not count words either. The persona's feedback calls the decision "disproportionate".

The cost was one extra decision, not an extra round. It was bundled into the draft-ready reply alongside the review-rule question.

retail-A (Codex agent, Claude persona):
- In msg 7 the user wrote a 16-word headline ("Top 10% of customers bring 54% of revenue; 41% of new customers reorder within 90 days.") and in the same message told the agent to go ahead with the full draft.
- Reply 7 kept it "verbatim" without mentioning its length. The draft and release 001 manifests each have one `accepted_long_headlines` entry. Its reason was written by the agent ("The user explicitly requested this headline…"), not given by the user.
- The friction log (agent-notes.md:115, 117, 120) confirms the agent was "avoiding a redundant length question".
- This is the agent's own choice on the same skill, not a harness effect. Nothing in the harness note pushes toward fewer questions.
- However, a preview-stage counter would not have caught this one. The headline was written after the preview, and there was no second preview. What retail-A actually shows is different: SKILL.md:83 says the warning row is "asked about", and the manifest template says the reason must be the user's. The agent skipped the ask, recorded a reason it inferred as the user's, and never told the user the headline was over the limit.

Bookkeeping: the finding cites retail-B-07 and retail-A-18, but in each run's findings.json those IDs are different findings (the reconciliation-table chart swap and a reviewloop measurement gap). The matching entries are retail-B-05 and retail-A-12. The underlying transcript evidence matches the claims.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-package/SKILL.md:54 tells the agent to say "a headline holds at most 15 words" at the headline checkpoint, but gives it no way to count.
- awb-package/SKILL.md:49 says `.preview/headlines.md` is a file "which no check reads".
- awb_draft.py: the comment around line 46 and the inventory code around lines 1802 and 1819 keep `.preview/` out of check-draft and release.
- awb_draft.py:1901 sets HEADLINE_WORDS = 15, and lines 2153-2160 raise the long-headline warning. This only runs in check-draft on findings.md, after the full draft.
- awb-package/SKILL.md:83 says a long-headline warning row "is asked about as the headline checkpoint says".
- manifest-template.md:68 says the `accepted_long_headlines` reason "is the user's reason". The retail-A agent did not follow this.
verdicts.narrowed: Only retail-B supports the finding as stated. The release never measures headline length during preview-and-wait. SKILL.md:54 has the agent state the 15-word limit, and `.preview/` is excluded from every check. So the agent can tell the user every headline fits when one does not: retail-B's approved headline 4 had 16 words. That headline then came back as an extra decision at check-draft. It was bundled into the draft-ready reply, so it cost a decision but not a separate round. retail-A shows a different, product-side deviation that a preview counter would not have prevented. The user wrote a 16-word headline after the preview. The Codex agent kept it without saying it was over the limit or asking, and recorded a reason it inferred in `accepted_long_headlines`, although SKILL.md:83 and manifest-template.md:68 call for asking and for the user's own reason.

verdicts.reasoning:
Only the retail-B half of this finding holds. retail-A doesn't show the defect.

retail-B shows the defect. Reply 3 says "Each headline is at most 15 words." Reply 4 repeats "each at most 15 words", but headline 4 is unchanged: "Top 10% of identified customers: 64% of identified revenue, 55% of total; 13% lacks an ID". That headline has 16 whitespace words. Message 5 approved it. In agent-005, check-draft's outline row reads "the headline has 16 words, over the 15-word limit ... accepted: false". Because of SKILL.md:54 and :83 (ask before trimming a headline the user approved, never trim it unasked), the agent had to ask again. It did, as Decision 1 in reply 5, and the user chose the shorter wording in message 6. The agent's own turn notes say: "Preview step could run the word count to catch this earlier (I miscounted)."

The release causes this:
- **No check at the preview:** the preview is deliberately left unchecked. SKILL.md:49 puts it in `.preview/headlines.md`, "which no check reads", and package-contract.md:19 repeats that.
- **Word count exists only in check-draft:** the only word counter is `outline_problems` (`_words`, `HEADLINE_WORDS`, awb_draft.py:1901 and 2154-2159). It reads `findings.md` at check-draft. There is no helper or command that counts words in the preview.
- **The instruction invites an unchecked claim:** SKILL.md:54 tells the agent to "say in one sentence ... that a headline holds at most 15 words". It never tells the agent to count its preview headlines. So the agent states the limit as if every headline met it, with nothing to confirm it.

Language models miscount words often, so a real user would hit this from time to time. Once the user approves a miscounted headline, the ask-before-trimming rule forces a second decision at check-draft.

The cost is small. The extra decision was folded into a round that was happening anyway, since message 6 also asked for two other corrections, so it did not add a round. Severity is minor.

retail-A doesn't support the claim. Its preview was within the limit: reply 6 lists headlines of 14 words or fewer. The 16-word headline was one the user wrote in message 7: "Top 10% of customers bring 54% of revenue; 41% of new customers reorder within 90 days." That came after the preview, together with "go ahead with the full draft", so no word count at the preview could have caught it. No extra decision came of it. Instead the agent wrote an `accepted_long_headlines` entry itself, without asking, giving a reason it inferred. Its notes call this "avoiding a redundant length question". That is the agent departing from manifest-template.md:68, which says the entry is for a headline "the user chose to keep" and that the "reason is the user's reason". It is not the cost the finding describes.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- **awb-package/SKILL.md:49:** the preview-and-wait headlines go in `.preview/headlines.md`, "which no check reads".
- **awb-package/SKILL.md:54:** "say in one sentence ... that a headline holds at most 15 words". It gives no instruction to count the preview headlines. It also says: "Before trimming a headline the user wrote or approved, ask ... recorded with their reason in the manifest's `accepted_long_headlines`."
- **awb-package/SKILL.md:83:** "a long-headline `warning` row is asked about as the headline checkpoint says, never trimmed unasked".
- **awb-package/references/package-contract.md:19:** the preview is "not inventoried, checked, or released".
- **awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py:1901 and 2093-2159:** `HEADLINE_WORDS = 15`. `_words` and `outline_problems` count words only in `findings.md`, at check-draft. No command or helper takes preview text.
- **manifest-template.md:68:** `accepted_long_headlines` is for headlines "the user chose to keep", with "the user's reason". retail-A broke this rule; the release did not cause it.
verdicts.narrowed: The preview step does not count headline words. The release leaves `.preview/headlines.md` unchecked, and SKILL.md:54 has the agent state the 15-word limit without telling it to count. In retail-B, a 16-word headline was approved after the agent claimed every headline had 15 words or fewer. check-draft's warning then needed a second decision, which was folded into a round that was happening anyway, so it cost no extra round. retail-A is not evidence for this: its long headline was written by the user after the preview, and the agent recorded the user's acceptance itself without asking.

consolidated.title: The review's closed readability list lets technical prose and typos through
consolidated.description: review.md's readability item checks 'only these': undefined glossary terms, excess decimals, record words and imperatives. check-draft catches only names spelled the workbench's way. retail-A's How we know slide and methods note reached the user with 'signed quantity', 'grouping keys' and 'permitted repeated line occurrences' after a full review. taxi-A's released findings.md has two double periods ('6 p.m..') from the 12-hour time conversion, which passed both the review and the check for the user's time-format rule.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: partly: #101 (issue #85) added the readability item as a closed list ('only these').
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-05: msg 8 correction 2; reply 8; the full-review report in relay/agent-007.jsonl lists 3 problems, none about these terms. taxi-A-16: storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/findings.md:23 and :60; .workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py:8. Release: awb-package/references/review.md:28.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and did not find one.

retail-A: the three phrases ('signed quantity', 'grouping keys' and 'permitted repeated line occurrences') were in the draft when the full review ran. relay/agent-008.jsonl shows the agent's replacement script rewriting exactly these lines: in findings.md the 'How we know' bullets and the slide-3 notes, and in methodology-note.md the Method section. The full-review report (review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt) lists three narrative problems: two uncited verification claims in methodology.md and one imperative. None concerns these phrases.

The brief the reviewer read already asked for plain wording. The copy of brief.md in agent-007.jsonl says the audience is 'commercially sharp and not technical' and the materials should 'avoid technical implementation details'. The release's findings-template.md:66 also tells the writer to give the 'How we know' method 'in plain language'. Yet review.md:28 limits readability to 'only these' four items, and step 4 says 'Report exactly this, and nothing else'. None of the phrases is a glossary term, so the reviewer obeyed the brief correctly by not flagging them. The release's own instructions caused the miss. The model did not drift.

The persona file (kit/personas/retail.md) mentions none of these terms. The simulated user found them by reading the draft, so the persona did not front-load the correction. The study note tells the agent to 'Work exactly as you normally would'. The reviewer was a real fresh Codex subagent: the log shows collab wait calls, and review-receipt start and record both ran. Codex is a supported host, and the review brief is the same on every host. A Claude Plan subagent given the same closed list would be told the same thing.

taxi-A: the agent's own script, .workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py:8, replaced '18:00' with '6 p.m.' using a regex. When the time ended a sentence, this left '6 p.m..'. The result is at findings.md:23 and :60 in both the draft and storage/releases/.../001, and also at methodology.md:61. The scoped review afterwards (agent-008-record01.txt) covered the changed lines and reported 'R-time-format-001 pass ... review (scoped): clean'. That rule's pattern only looks for 24-hour times, and no review item or check-draft step looks at punctuation. The simulated user approved the preview file without noticing the typo, which is a lapse by the simulated user. But the review gate would have passed the typo on any host, because nothing in it looks for one.

The typo itself comes from model behavior in the agent's script, not from the release. What the release causes is that the gate cannot catch it. The jargon half is clearly a product issue. The typo half is weaker: one instance, and no release check claims to proofread.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:28 limits readability checks to 'only these' (glossary terms, excess decimals, record words and IDs, imperatives), and step 4 says 'Report exactly this, and nothing else'. awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:66 tells the writer to give the 'How we know' method 'in plain language', but no review step checks this, nor the brief's Audience instruction to avoid technical detail. The project's review-rules.md R-time-format-001 pattern only finds 24-hour times, and nothing checks punctuation.
verdicts.narrowed: The review checks readability against a closed list only. Nothing checks the brief's Audience instruction to avoid technical detail or the template's plain-language requirement for the 'How we know' slide, and nothing checks for mechanical typos. So jargon and conversion typos the writing agent introduces reach the user after a review that passes. retail-A shows this firmly: the brief at review time said to 'avoid technical implementation details'. The typo half rests on one instance, and the typo came from a regex the agent wrote, not from the release. The release causes only that the review cannot catch it.

verdicts.reasoning:
Release text. awb-package/references/review.md:28 limits the reviewer's readability check to "readability, only these": glossary-defined terms used before they are defined, too many decimals, record words or IDs, and imperatives. Step 4 (review.md:29) then says "Report exactly this, and nothing else." The other step-3 checks (review.md:26-27) look at citations, claim strength and whether brief.md's question parts are answered. None of them looks at the brief's **Audience** style. So a reviewer that follows the brief may not flag jargon unless the glossary defines the term, even when the brief says the audience is non-technical. It has no remit for typos at all. check-draft's name check (helpers.md:27) only matches names spelled the workbench's way. On the drafting side, the release does tell the writer to write plainly: findings-template.md:5-7 ("use the terms they use, assume what they already know and nothing more"), :66 ("Give the method in plain language"), and methodology-note-template.md:5-9. The writing agent ignored that once. It was not repeated.

retail-A evidence holds. The brief's Audience was committed at 9096f84, before packaging: "Leadership team, commercially sharp and not technical ... avoid technical implementation details in the audience materials." In agent-008.jsonl, the How we know slide's pre-edit text was: "11,812 permitted repeated line occurrences retained", "Revenue is signed quantity × price in GBP", "Checks cover required fields, row counts ..., grouping keys and missing values". The note's Method section had the same terms. The full review is in agent-007 (review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt). It reported 3 problems: methodology.md:28 and :36 for missing citations, and findings.md:82 for an imperative. None of them is about these terms. "signed quantity" is not a defined term in foundation/glossary.md, so the closed glossary item could not catch it either. The user caught it in msg 8 correction 2, and the agent then added rule R-plain-language-001. The release is the reason the independent review missed it.

taxi-A evidence holds factually, but it is weaker. The released findings.md:23 reads "Both months peak at 6 p.m.." and :60 reads "27.65% at 6–7 p.m..". The cause is the agent's own ad-hoc script, .workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py:6-9. Its regex replaces "18:00" with "6 p.m." and leaves the sentence's own period in place. The scoped review (agent-008-record01.txt) judged those changed lines and reported "R-time-format-001 pass ... clean". The rule's pattern only matches 24-hour times, so it was never going to catch this. The release did not produce the typo. It only has no proofreading step, by design of the closed list.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:28 ("readability, only these, in findings.md and the note: ... glossary ... decimal places ... ledger, flagged, or disposition, a record ID ... imperative") and review.md:29 ("Report exactly this, and nothing else"): no check of Audience-appropriate wording beyond glossary-defined terms, and none of typos or punctuation. awb-package/references/helpers.md:27: check-draft's name rows cover only workbench-spelled names. Run evidence: retail-A/relay/agent-008.jsonl (pre-edit How we know and Method text containing the three terms), retail-A/review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt (full review, 3 unrelated problems), retail-A project brief.md Audience at commit 9096f84, retail-A transcript msg 8, taxi-A/storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/findings.md:23 and :60, taxi-A/project/.workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py:6-9, and taxi-A/review-reports/agent-008-record01.txt (scoped review clean).
verdicts.narrowed: The draft review's readability check is a closed list (review.md:28) with "nothing else" reporting (review.md:29). It leaves out jargon the glossary does not define, even when brief.md's Audience records a non-technical audience. In retail-A, a full independent review therefore passed a How we know slide and methodology note containing "signed quantity", "grouping keys" and "permitted repeated line occurrences", and only the user caught them. consolidated.title: Imperative-voice rule flags builder instructions and requested recommendations
consolidated.description: The readability rule against imperatives outside Implications flagged a chart-builder instruction in retail-A, which cost a repair and a second review. In retail-B it clashed with the user's request for a recommendation on the Answer slide, and produced the gerund headline 'Recommendation: protecting key accounts, testing retention alongside acquisition'.
consolidated.oct16_ref: new; side effect of the C-33 fix (#85)
consolidated.caused_by_fix: yes: #101 (issue #85) added the imperative item with no exemption for chart specifications or for a labelled recommendation.
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-19: the full-review record in relay/agent-007.jsonl (findings.md:82). retail-B-05: msg 4; agent-005 full review (findings.md:7 and :12); release 001 findings.md. Release: review.md:28; findings-template.md (Implications).

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not find a harness cause. The rule comes from the release, two different reviewer setups applied it literally, and the user requests behind both flags are ones a real user would make.

The release cause: review.md:28 tells the reviewer to flag "a sentence in the imperative ... outside **Implications**" anywhere in findings.md. It makes no exception for chart-specification fields or for a recommendation on the Answer slide. Nothing in findings-template.md exempts them either: Implications is optional, and the Answer slide is "the answer to the question".

retail-A (Codex agent and Codex reviewer subagent): review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt flags findings.md:82 "keep the saved ranking by GBP increase", the chart-axis field. It was repaired to "countries ranked by GBP increase", which is the text in released/001/findings.md:82. The wording traces to the user's own words ("Keep the £ ranking and the Japan/Norway bases in the body", agent-007.in.md) and to brief.md:49 ("Keep Q5 ranked by GBP increase"). That is ordinary user speech, not persona front-loading.

retail-B (Claude agent, read-only Plan reviewer): review-reports/agent-005-record01.txt flags findings.md:7 "Protect key accounts, test retention alongside acquisition" and findings.md:12 as imperatives outside Implications. The simulated user had asked for this in plain terms. Message 4 says "Please ensure the Answer slide gives a cautious commercial recommendation". Message 5 says "Recommend protecting key accounts and testing retention alongside acquisition". The agent rewrote it as gerunds and told the user "the deck rules don't allow commands on that slide". The gerund headline is in storage/releases/.../001/findings.md:7, and the deck has no Implications slide.

Harness factors I checked and ruled out:
- Non-interactive operation: it affects neither the reviewer's verdict nor the release text.
- Reviewer setup: a Codex subagent and a Claude Plan subagent both flagged the same rule.
- Study disclosure: it only affects how strongly the agents describe the problem in feedback. Both outcomes exist as artifacts: the review reports and the released findings.md.
- Relay, sandbox and simulated home: none of them are involved.

Where the finding overstates:
1. Neither flag cost an extra review cycle. retail-A's first full review also had two methodology.md narrative problems (lines 28 and 36), and retail-B's had 13 other narrative problems. A scoped re-review was required either way, so the retail-A cost was a one-line rewording.
2. The retail-A flag is arguably harmless or even an improvement. The template defines the Axis field as descriptive ("<unit, and zero baseline ...>"), and the chart file's row order already fixes the ranking.
3. In retail-B the rule does not block a recommendation, only the imperative mood. "We recommend protecting key accounts and testing retention alongside acquisition" would pass. The awkward gerund was the agent's choice of repair, though a real agent could easily choose it too. The simulated user approved the result and never objected (messages 6–8, human.md).
4. Retail-B's agent.md labels this "Major". That reflects the agent's tone under the study framing, not the impact.
verdicts.release_evidence:
These are under SIMS/.
- release/analytics-workbench-skills/awb-package/references/review.md:28: the readability rule flags a sentence in the imperative "outside **Implications**" in findings.md and the note, with no exemption for chart-spec fields or for a user-requested recommendation.
- review.md:43: in awb-package the agent repairs every narrative problem from the first review, with no step that sends user-requested wording back to the user.
- release/.../package-format/findings-template.md:32-42: the Answer slide has no recommendation element.
- findings-template.md:52-58: Implications is optional and is where recommendations go.
- Observed results: retail-A/review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt (findings.md:82 flag, repaired in released/001/findings.md:82); retail-B/review-reports/agent-005-record01.txt (findings.md:7 and :12 flags); retail-B/storage/releases/marketing-budget-evidence/leadership-deck/001/findings.md:7 and :12 (gerund recommendation in the release).
verdicts.narrowed: The release's rule against imperatives outside Implications (review.md:28) has no exemption for chart-spec fields or for a recommendation the user asked for on the Answer slide. Reviewers on both hosts apply it literally. In retail-B this pushed user-requested recommendation wording into an awkward gerund headline that shipped in release 001. A declarative "We recommend..." would have passed, so the poor phrasing was partly the agent's repair choice. In retail-A it flagged a builder instruction in the chart Axis field, which took a trivial one-line rewording. Neither flag caused an extra review cycle, because both first reviews had other narrative problems that required a scoped re-review anyway. Severity: minor, mostly about the quality of the shipped wording.

verdicts.reasoning:
The release causes the flag. No shipped code checks for imperatives (grep finds the rule only in review.md and CHANGELOG). The only source is the reviewer brief, review.md:28. It applies readability "in `findings.md` and the note" and lists "a sentence in the imperative ... outside **Implications**". Nothing exempts the Answer slide or the chart-specification fields.

retail-B: the evidence holds. In msg 4 the user asked that "the Answer slide gives a cautious commercial recommendation on retention versus acquisition", and msg 5 supplied the wording ("Recommend protecting key accounts and testing retention alongside acquisition"). The agent-005 full review (review-reports/agent-005-record01.txt) flagged findings.md:7 "Protect key accounts, test retention alongside acquisition" and :12 "Recommendation: protect key accounts..." as imperatives outside Implications. review.md:43 tells awb-package to repair every narrative problem rather than ask, so the agent reworded without asking. It told the user "the deck rules don't allow commands on that slide". The shipped release (storage/releases/.../001/findings.md:7) carries "Recommendation: protecting key accounts, testing retention alongside acquisition; top 10%...". The release's own templates put recommendations in the optional Implications slide; the required Answer slide template asks for no recommendation. So a user who wants the recommendation on the Answer slide, which is common, will run into this rule. The awkward gerund was the agent's choice, though. A declarative "We recommend protecting key accounts..." would have met both the rule and the request. The user did not object, and in msg 6 said they were "happy with ... the cautious commercial recommendations".

retail-A: the flagged text existed, but the finding overstates the cost. The Codex rollout shows findings.md:82 was the Chart 4 spec field "- **Axis:** Net revenue increase (GBP), zero baseline; keep the saved ranking by GBP increase". deck-rules.md treats **Axis:** as text for the builder, not the audience: axis titles come from the file header, and the field is read only for baseline wording. So the flag targeted text no audience member sees, a mild false positive against the rule's purpose. The instruction was also redundant: deck-rules.md already says Horizontal bars plot "categories in the file's order", and the template's Axis field is for unit and baseline. The repair was a one-line edit. The second, scoped review is not attributable to this flag. The same full review (agent-007-record01) also reported two methodology.md narrative problems (:28, :36) that needed repair and a re-review anyway.

Verdict: the release causes it, but it is cosmetic. "Cost a second review" does not hold for retail-A, and the awkward gerund in retail-B is one agent's way of complying, not something the rule required.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md:28 (the readability item covers all of findings.md and the note; "a sentence in the imperative ('Exclude refunds' for 'Refunds were excluded') outside **Implications**"; no exemption for the Answer slide or chart-spec fields). awb-package/references/review.md:43 (in awb-package, "repair every ... narrative problem", so the agent repairs without asking the user). awb-package/assets/package-format/findings-template.md:36-42 (the Answer slide holds the question, findings and qualification, with no recommendation) and :52-58 (recommendations go in the optional Implications slide). findings-template.md:25 (Axis field = unit and baseline). awb-package/assets/package-format/deck-rules.md:44, 57, 72 (bars follow the file's order; axis titles come from the file header; the builder reads Axis only for baseline wording, so it is builder-facing). No imperative check in awb_draft.py or any other code. Run evidence: retail-A review-reports/agent-007-record01.txt (flag at findings.md:82 next to two methodology problems); Codex rollout 01a14995 lines 1108 and 1206 (original Axis line and its one-line repair). retail-B transcript msg 4 and msg 5 (user asks for an Answer-slide recommendation), review-reports/agent-005-record01.txt (findings.md:7 and :12 flagged), storage/releases/marketing-budget-evidence/leadership-deck/001/findings.md:7 and :12 (the gerund wording shipped).
verdicts.narrowed: The review brief's imperative rule (review.md:28) covers everything in findings.md outside Implications, including the required Answer slide. It therefore flags a recommendation the user explicitly asked for there, and because review.md:43 says to repair every narrative problem, the agent rewords user-requested wording without asking. In retail-B that produced, and shipped, an awkward gerund headline, though a declarative "We recommend ..." would have complied. The rule also reaches builder-facing chart-spec fields such as **Axis:**, which the audience never sees. In retail-A that was a harmless one-line edit; the follow-up review there was needed anyway for two methodology problems, so the claim that the flag cost a second review does not hold. Cosmetic severity.

consolidated.title: The deliverable is a builder kit, not a rendered deck
consolidated.description: The package is a Markdown outline, chart CSVs and assembly instructions. The one-page note has a word-count check but no layout check. co2-A's user must build the deck within a 10-day window. The README discloses this and both users accepted it, so the evidence of harm is weak.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-29: storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/; msg 10. co2-A-18: r6, m9; human.md section 6. README 'What you get'.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not tie this to the harness. The package format comes from the release's design, and it comes out the same on both hosts. All six runs released the same kind of package: findings.md, charts/*.csv, deck-rules.md, assembly/m365.md, START-HERE.md, manifest.json, methodology.md and methodology-note.md, with no .pptx and nothing rendered. That holds for the Codex-agent runs (A), which used the sandbox, non-interactive exec and auto-approved MCP. It also holds for the Claude Code runs (B). The README's first statement under "What you get" is that the package "is not a .pptx. Nothing in the workbench draws slides." None of the awb-package skill text offers a rendering step that the sandbox could have blocked. A real user on any host gets the same kit.

I checked each harness factor:
- **Persona briefs.** They ask for "a deck of about 8 slides plus a one-page methodology note," which is what a real user would ask for. They did not create the mismatch.
- **README reading.** The harness had each persona read the README before its first message. If anything, that makes the sim understate the expectation gap, since real users who skip the README depend only on the agent's wording.
- **The friction log.** The study's friction-log request did prompt the Codex agents' critiques. In taxi-A the only source is the agent (agent.md item 13). The user there accepted the kit ("I'll build the deck from START-HERE", msg 10) and only noted that findings.md is "hard to picture as slides." That affects who raised the point, not whether it is true.
- **Where the sim stops.** Every run ends at release. Nobody builds the deck, so any harm downstream is never observed.

Harm evidence is weak, as the finding itself says:
- co2-A's "extra work in a 10-day window" (human.md section 6) is the persona guessing ahead. Its own notes say "I may build by hand; that's fine."
- co2-B and check-A users said the README's "deck package, not a .pptx" disclosure set their expectations correctly.
- The "no layout check" claim is accurate: check-draft compares the note's length with the brief's Audience length, and gives no page check. But a Markdown note has no page layout until someone renders it, and no run shows it overflowing a page. taxi-A's user accepted 521 words as one page.

Smaller observed friction: co2-A's agent ended reply 6 with "next: build the PowerPoint from the package." The user found it unclear who that job belonged to (human notes; human.md pain point 8).

The finding cites taxi-A-29, but the matching entry in taxi-A/feedback/findings.json is taxi-A-20. That looks like a renumbering slip and does not affect the substance.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- README.md, "What you get", line 11: "a folder of files that a deck is built from. It is not a .pptx. Nothing in the workbench draws slides." Lines 24-29 give the Copilot and by-hand build routes.
- awb-package/assets/package-format/methodology-note-template.md: the note length is checked against "the methods note length the brief's Audience records, which check-draft compares, or to a page or two when it records none." There is no page or layout check.
- The released folders taxi-A/storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/ and co2-A/storage/releases/emissions-and-country-focus/donor-roundtable/001/ hold only Markdown, CSV and JSON. The B-variant (Claude Code host) releases in taxi-B, co2-B and retail-B have the same structure.
- co2-A reply 6 ends with "next: build the PowerPoint from the package."
verdicts.narrowed: This is a disclosed scope limit, not an observed defect. By design the release delivers a builder kit (Markdown outline, chart CSVs, deck rules, M365 assembly steps) rather than a rendered .pptx. Its audience methods note is Markdown, and only its word count is checked against the brief, never its rendered page length. Every user on every host gets this. The README and START-HERE disclose it, and every user in these runs accepted it. Building the deck and fitting the note on one page are left to the user, and the sim ends at release before either happens, so any cost under a deadline is unobserved. The co2-A cost is the persona's prediction, and the taxi-A point was raised only by the agent. One small piece of product friction was observed in co2-A: the agent's closing line "next: build the PowerPoint from the package" did not say that the user, not the agent, does that step.

verdicts.reasoning:
The package is a builder kit and not a rendered deck. That much is accurate, but it is the release's stated design, and nothing in the cited evidence shows a user was misled or harmed by it.

Release text that prevents the expectation gap:
- README "What you get", line 11: "It is not a .pptx. Nothing in the workbench draws slides."
- The same section lists every file in the package and gives both build routes: Copilot with the PowerPoint agent, or by hand.
- README "What you will be asked", item 5, discloses the word-count proxy: a methods-note length such as "one page" is recorded as a word count, "about 500 to a page", and the check reports a note more than 10% over it.
- awb-package step 7 tells the agent to point the user to START-HERE.md. That file tells the user plainly that they build the deck themselves.
- Both simulated users received a README identical to the release README (diff shows no difference).

Run evidence:
- taxi-A: the user asked for "about 8 slides plus a one-page methodology note". In their feedback (human.md section 1) they called the 521-word note one that "fits the one page I asked for". Their final message (human-010) was "I'll build the deck from START-HERE." They raised no complaint about the format. The issue comes only from the agent's self-report (agent.md section 1 item 13). The cited ID taxi-A-29 does not exist; the matching finding is taxi-A-20.
- co2-A: agent-006 (r6) links to START-HERE as "PowerPoint assembly and delivery instructions". human-009 (m9) accepts the release and says "I'll build the deck from START-HERE." Human.md section 6 calls the 489-word note "right-sized (489 words, one page)". The user's only objection is "no .pptx ... The README is upfront about this, but it's extra work in a 10-day window." That asks for a renderer the release never claims to have. Their notes.md also says building by hand is "fine".

"No layout check" is not a gap in the release. The note is Markdown and has no layout to check, and the word-count stand-in is disclosed. No agent ignored an instruction. No user misunderstood the deliverable or lost time to a misunderstanding. The finding itself concedes the evidence of harm is weak.

A related item is separate and is not this finding: co2-A pain point 8 says the agent's "next: build the PowerPoint" line was briefly unclear about who builds the deck. That is about the agent's wording, not the format of the deliverable.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- README.md line 11 ("What you get"): "It is not a .pptx. Nothing in the workbench draws slides."
- The same section lists each file in the package and both build routes, Copilot PowerPoint agent or by hand.
- README "What you will be asked", item 5: "one page" is recorded as a word count, about 500 words to a page, and the check flags a note more than 10% over it.
- awb-package/SKILL.md step 7: point the user to START-HERE.md, which covers what to send, what builds the deck in Copilot, and what stays internal.
- Released START-HERE.md (taxi-A storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/START-HERE.md): "the deck, once you build it as part 2 says".
- human/README.md is byte-identical to the release README in both runs.
verdicts.narrowed: Feature request only, not a defect: by disclosed design the release has no rendering step (.pptx or a paginated PDF note), so a user who needs a finished deck builds it from START-HERE, by hand or with Copilot. The README states this up front, and both users read it, accepted it, and confirmed their notes fit one page.

consolidated.title: File links switch to relative paths, including for the release copy
consolidated.description: From reply 6 on, retail-A gave the drafts and the release copy as relative links (../storage/releases/...). awb-release asks for the full path, and the release tool had returned it as an absolute path. co2-A switched to project-relative links in r7, and the user feared they would not open. Tag: co2-A-21 is unclear; retail-A-06 is product, because the agent skipped a required full path that the helper supplied.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no. #103 made release's storage row an absolute path; the agent did not use it.
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-06: replies 6-9; absolute storage.path in relay/agent-009.jsonl against agent-009.last.md; awb-release/SKILL.md section 5. co2-A-21: r7; human.md pain point 7.

verdicts.reasoning:
This is not a harness artifact. I checked every harness channel I could and none caused the link switch. Codex compaction set off the timing, but the release instruction was still broken on a host a real user would have.

What triggered the switch:
- In both Codex-agent runs, the switch from absolute to project-relative links lands in the exact turn where Codex auto-compacted the context.
- retail-A: rollout line 944, `compacted` in turn 6 at about 286k of 475k tokens. Turns 1-5 used only absolute link targets. Turns 6-9 used only relative ones (`deliveries/...`, `../agent-home/...`, `../storage/releases/...`).
- co2-A: compaction in turn 7. Turns 1-6 were absolute, turn 7 was relative.

Why that is not harness-specific:
- The context filled with release material: AGENTS.md, workbench guides, skill files, result reads and a chart image. The study's friction-log note adds very little.
- An interactive Codex session running the same workflow on the same model would compact at the same point.
- The relay passes text through verbatim; agent-009.last.md already holds the relative link. The relay runs `codex exec resume` in the project folder, which is the same as an interactive thread. Sandbox, MCP auto-approval and the simulated home have no bearing on how links are written.
- Codex's own base instructions, in the session_meta `base_instructions`, require markdown file links with an absolute target. So nothing in the host or harness pushed the agent toward relative links. The model drifted after compaction.

Would a real user hit it?
- Yes. On a real host the user would see only the link label `marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/`, and the relative target may not be clickable. That is no better than the raw text the simulated user read.

Is the release the cause?
- Only in a limited sense. awb-release section 5 says plainly to report the storage row's full `path`. The helper returned it as an absolute path. The agent re-read awb-release/SKILL.md in turn 9 and still turned the path into `../storage/...`.
- So the release text has no defect. Its instruction failed to hold on its target host. The release's large context footprint makes that compaction-driven drift likely mid-workflow.

The co2-A half is weaker:
- The r7 relative links were draft links only. In r8 the agent reported the release copy's full absolute path in a code block, after the user asked for it.
- The simulated user's worry that relative links "may not open from my terminal" comes from reading raw markdown.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- **Release instruction:** awb-release/SKILL.md section 5 says "Report the `storage` row: the full `path` of the release's copy in storage".
- **README promise:** README line 31 says the agent "reports the copy's full path".
- **Helper output:** retail-A/relay/agent-009.jsonl, the awb/release result, returns storage.path as the absolute path `<tmp>/.../retail-A/storage/releases/marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/`.
- **Agent reply:** agent-009.last.md gives `[marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/](../storage/releases/marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/)`.
- **Instruction freshly read:** the agent ran `cat .../awb-release/SKILL.md` in the same turn.
- **Codex's own rule:** base instructions in rollout-...01a14995-3812...jsonl say "Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target".
- **Compaction timing:** rollout `compacted` events are in retail-A turn 6 (line 944) and co2-A turn 7 (line 944). Every assistant link before them has an absolute target; every one after them is relative.
- **Users' reactions:**
  - retail-A/feedback/human.md pain point 5 flags relative paths and the missing full path at release.
  - co2-A/feedback/human.md pain point 7 is about inconsistent draft links only.
  - In co2-A r8 the agent gave the full release path.
verdicts.narrowed:
Only retail-A supports the release-copy claim:
- After Codex auto-compacted the agent's context mid-session (retail-A turn 6), the agent used only project-relative file links.
- That included the release copy in reply 9, even though awb-release section 5 requires the full storage path, the release helper returned it as an absolute path, and the agent had just re-read the skill.
- The trigger is model drift after compaction on the Codex host, not wording in the release. A real interactive Codex user running this context-heavy workflow would hit it too.

co2-A only shows inconsistent draft links after its own compaction in r7. Its release reply gave the full path, and the simulated user's worry that the links "may not open" rests on reading raw markdown.

verdicts.reasoning:
Release copy: the shipped release already asks for the full path, so it prevents this rather than causing it. awb-release/SKILL.md section 5 says "Report the `storage` row: the full `path` of the release's copy in storage". The README (line 31) also promises the agent "reports the copy's full path". The helper returned the path as absolute: in retail-A relay/agent-009.jsonl, storage.path = <tmp>/.../retail-A/storage/releases/marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/. In that same turn the agent cat'd awb-release/SKILL.md. It still wrote "[marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/](../storage/releases/marketing-budget/leadership-budget/001/)" (agent-009.last.md). That is one agent ignoring a clear instruction once; retail-A made only one release. The other five runs followed the instruction and reported the absolute release path: taxi-A r9, co2-A r8 and co2-B r6 (agent-*.last.md / .out.md), plus taxi-B r7 and retail-B r7. Three of these, taxi-A, co2-A and retail-A, used the same Codex agent setup. co2-A's human wrote "the full path reported" for the release. So the finding title's "including for the release copy" is true for retail-A only.

Draft links: the release does not say whether draft links should be absolute or relative. AGENTS.md says "Answer in chat, giving file paths" and awb-package's Report says "the draft path". So the agent chose its own link style and switched within runs: retail-A was absolute in r4-5 and relative from r6; co2-A was absolute in r6 and relative in r7. Nothing in the release pushes the agent toward relative links. Project-relative links resolve correctly against the project root (../storage/... does point at the storage folder). On normal interactive hosts, where the session's working folder is the project, they generally open. The evidence of harm is weak. co2-A pain point 7 is a guess ("may not open from my terminal"). The retail-A human "had to work out the full path", but that human was a simulated persona reading relayed text files with no host to click links in. None of this is a release-caused defect a real user would reliably hit. The co2-A-21 part shows only inconsistent draft links, not a broken release-copy path.
verdicts.release_evidence:
These are under SIMS/release/analytics-workbench-skills/:
- awb-release/SKILL.md section 5: "Report the `storage` row: the full `path` of the release's copy in storage and whether the copy verified". This instruction prevents the release-copy problem.
- README.md line 31: "...and reports the copy's full path."
- awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md (Conversation section): "Answer in chat, giving file paths". It does not say absolute or relative.
- awb-package/SKILL.md line 96 (Report): "the draft path". It does not say absolute or relative.

Run evidence:
- retail-A relay/agent-009.jsonl: the helper returned an absolute storage.path, and the agent read awb-release/SKILL.md in that turn. agent-009.last.md still gives a relative link.
- The other five runs reported the absolute release path: co2-A agent-008.last.md, taxi-A agent-009.last.md, taxi-B agent-007.out.md, co2-B agent-006.out.md, retail-B agent-007.out.md.
verdicts.narrowed: The release copy is a one-off agent miss, not a product defect: in retail-A only, the agent ignored awb-release section 5's clear "full path" instruction once, even though the helper supplied the absolute path. A narrow, cosmetic point does hold. The release never says whether draft links in chat should be absolute or project-relative: AGENTS.md says only "giving file paths" and awb-package says "the draft path". As a result, draft-link style changed within a run (retail-A from r6, co2-A in r7). If consistent links matter, one sentence in AGENTS.md's Conversation section asking for absolute paths would settle it. The evidence does not show a user on a normal host being unable to open the links.

consolidated.title: TLC documentation downloads: a real 403 for curl, and one agent faked a browser user agent
consolidated.description: In taxi-A, curl got HTTP 403 from nyc.gov for the data dictionary and data page. The Codex web reader could read them, and the agent recorded access notes, which awb-status reported as known limitations. In taxi-B the agent fetched the PDF with a browser user agent (-A 'Mozilla/5.0') without first trying the default.
consolidated.oct16_ref: C-76 (#92; the handling is fixed); C-103 (harness)
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-32: reply 1; agent-notes line 11. taxi-B-32: curl call in relay/agent-003.jsonl; persona premise in human/BRIEF.md.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding has two halves. Neither one shows a fault in the release.

(1) The taxi-A 403 is real and did not come from the harness. The taxi-A agent was Codex with workspace-write and network_access = true, and its config sets no proxy. Both curl -fL calls exited 22 with "The requested URL returned error: 403". I sent HEAD requests to both URLs from this host, outside the Codex sandbox. Both returned 403 with curl's default user agent and 200 with "Mozilla/5.0". So nyc.gov filters on user agent, and a real user's agent running curl on a normal machine would get the same 403. The sandbox, the simulated home and the relay did not cause it. The release is not the cause either, and it handled the 403 the way it is built to. workbench-guides/data.md tells agents to write an access note for "a download the server refuses". The foundation/sources.md template even uses an HTTP 403 as its example. The agent wrote access notes of the form "read at <URL> on 2026-10-17, not kept: curl download refused with HTTP 403" for tlc-yellow and tlc-zones. The awb status output listed both under sources.documentation_access_notes and left documentation_without_reference empty. That is the designed limitation path, so this is correct behavior, not a defect.

(2) The taxi-B user-agent spoof was a model choice, and the persona primed it. taxi-B's agent was claude -p. The persona brief says "the site blocked the download". The human passed that on in message 1 ("I couldn't download the TLC data dictionary") and again in message 3 ("If it remains inaccessible, state what couldn't be verified"). The harness's agent system prompt only lets the agent open URLs the user gives it. So the agent asked for permission in reply 2, and the human's answer repeated that the site was inaccessible. The agent's first and only fetch then used -A "Mozilla/5.0" (it returned 200, application/pdf, 148556 bytes). It never tried the default user agent and never used WebFetch. No release text tells it to set a user agent. The release text points the other way: a refused download gets an access note. The persona premise is also out of line with reality, because a browser user gets 200 and would have been able to download the PDF. The spoof therefore comes from model behavior plus a front-loaded persona premise. It occurred in one run.

Overall: the 403 is real-world but outside the release, and the release handled it correctly. The spoof is harness- and model-driven. Neither part supports a release defect.
verdicts.release_evidence:
These release files show the designed handling for a refused documentation download:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md line 11: keep each dictionary under foundation/references/<source-id>/; documentation "you could read but not keep, such as a download the server refuses, gets an access note instead".
- awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/sources.md line 20: example access note "not kept: the server refused downloads (HTTP 403)"; "Status reports it as a known limitation."
- awb-init/references/landing.md line 59.
- CHANGELOG.md line 71: the access-note reference form, which status lists under sources.documentation_access_notes.
- awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py around line 318.

Run evidence:
- taxi-A, relay/agent-001.jsonl: both curl calls exit 22 with 403; the web reader opened both pages.
- taxi-A, agent-notes line 11.
- taxi-A, project/foundation/sources.md rows tlc-yellow and tlc-zones: the access notes.
- taxi-A, awb status result: documentation_access_notes ["tlc-yellow","tlc-zones"].
- taxi-B, relay/agent-003.jsonl: the single call curl -sSL -A "Mozilla/5.0" returned 200.
- taxi-B, relay/agent-001.in.md and agent-003.in.md: the human says the download failed and might stay inaccessible.
- taxi-B, human/BRIEF.md: "the site blocked the download".
- taxi-B, prompts/claude-agent-system.md: the agent may only open URLs the user gives it.

Independent check from this host: HEAD requests to both nyc.gov URLs returned 403 with curl's default user agent and 200 with -A "Mozilla/5.0".
verdicts.narrowed: nyc.gov returns 403 to curl's default user agent and 200 to a browser user agent, on any host, not only in the sandbox. The release's access-note path handled this as designed in taxi-A. The only release-related gap is guidance: data.md tells agents to keep a copy of each dictionary and to write an access note when the server refuses a download. It says nothing about whether to work around a refusal, for example by spoofing a browser user agent. In one run, after the persona premise said the download was blocked, a Claude agent spoofed a user agent without first trying the default. That is one occurrence of a possible documentation clarification driven by model behavior, not a product defect.

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence matches what the finding describes, but nothing in the release causes the behaviour, and the taxi-A half is the release working as designed.

taxi-A (Codex agent): in relay/agent-001.jsonl, `curl -fL` for the data dictionary PDF and for the trip-record page both exit 22 with HTTP 403. The agent then read both through the web reader. It wrote access notes in the exact form the release ships (sources.md line 8: "read at https://www.nyc.gov/site/tlc/... on 2026-10-17, not kept: curl download refused with HTTP 403"). agent-notes line 11 records the same, and status reported them as known limitations. The shipped files tell the agent to do exactly this:
- workbench-guides/data.md: "Documentation you could read but not keep, such as a download the server refuses, gets an access note instead."
- foundation/sources.md template: its example is literally `not kept: the server refused downloads (HTTP 403)`, followed by "Status reports it as a known limitation."
- awb-status (collect_status.py `documentation_access_notes`) lists these sources as a known limitation, not as missing a reference.
So taxi-A shows a real external 403 handled the way the release intends. It is not a defect.

taxi-B (Claude agent): relay/agent-003.jsonl shows that the first and only nyc.gov request was `curl -sSL ... -A "Mozilla/5.0"`, which returned 200 application/pdf. No request with curl's default user agent was made in turns 001 to 003. The finding is factually right there. However:
- A grep of the whole release for user-agent/Mozilla/curl/wget guidance finds nothing that suggests faking a user agent.
- Before that call the agent had read data.md and the sources.md template (agent-002, lines 2 and 11). Those files point a refused download to an access note.
- What set it up was the persona premise in human/BRIEF.md ("the site blocked the download"), which the simulated user repeated in agent-003.in.md ("If it remains inaccessible, state what couldn't be verified").
- The agent faked the browser up front on its own initiative. The harness's "URLs the user gives you" rule (kit/claude-agent-system.md) explains why it asked permission first, not the user-agent choice.

This is a single model choice in one run. It did not repeat, and the release did not prompt it. The retained PDF with its SHA-256 is arguably better provenance than an access note.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md, "Assess and acquire": "Documentation you could read but not keep, such as a download the server refuses, gets an access note instead, in the form given there."
- awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/sources.md, line 20: the access-note example `reference: read at https://example.org/dictionary.pdf on 2026-10-16, not kept: the server refused downloads (HTTP 403)`, followed by "Status reports it as a known limitation."
- awb-init/references/landing.md, line 59: the access-note grammar.
- awb-status/scripts/collect_status.py, lines 463-467: `documentation_access_notes`.
- No release file mentions user agents, Mozilla, or retrying a refused download with a browser identity.

Run evidence:
- taxi-A/relay/agent-001.jsonl: CMD exit 22, curl 403 on both URLs.
- taxi-A/project/foundation/sources.md, lines 7-8: the access notes.
- taxi-B/relay/agent-003.jsonl: `curl -sSL -A "Mozilla/5.0" ...` returned "200 application/pdf 148556". No earlier request with the default user agent.
- taxi-B/relay/agent-002.jsonl: data.md and the sources.md template were read before the curl call.
verdicts.narrowed: The release only partly covers this. data.md sends a refused download to an access note, but it never says not to get around a refusal, for example by retrying with a faked browser user agent. In one run (taxi-B), a Claude agent that had been told the site blocks downloads faked a browser user agent on its first request instead of trying the default and falling back to an access note. A one-line hardening in data.md would close this ("do not retry a refused download with a browser user agent or other workaround; record an access note"). This is a guidance gap, not a defect the release causes.

consolidated.title: What was agreed at the headline preview does not carry into the draft
consolidated.description: retail-B's preview dropped the agreed 'first observed' wording ('new 2010 customers'; 'December had only 76 new customers'), though the agent's own brief recorded it. Reply 3 promised a Year 1 / Year 2 / 24-month reconciliation table; the draft drew a 24-month bar chart instead. Nothing records what was agreed at the preview, or checks the preview against the brief.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: retail-B-04: msg 2; reply 3 headlines 5 and 8; brief.md line 62; msg 4; R-customer-terms-001 (reply 6). retail-B-10: reply 3; reply 5 chart 2; msg 6.

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none. The agent ran as one resumed claude -p session (relay.py:150 passes --resume with a fixed session id). None of the eight agent logs has a compact_boundary event, so the agent had the whole conversation in context when it drafted. The table promise came from the agent, not from a persona front-loading answers. Reply 3 promised it, and the agent wrote it into its own preview file at turn 4: `.preview/headlines.md` line 10 reads "(chart: table, components by year)". Codex playing the user did not shape the draft. MCP auto-approval and the study disclosure have nothing to do with how charts were picked.

**Table half (holds; release cause).** At turn 5 the agent exported `revenue-reconciliation:component,net_revenue@where=period=24 months`. Then `findings.md` specified "Horizontal bar: net revenue by component over the 24 months". The result at that point was long-form: period, component, net_revenue (git 7c155f6). `export` can pick columns and filter rows but cannot pivot. deck-rules.md:50 limits a Table to about six numbers or a two-way grid. awb-package/SKILL.md:10 and :69 say packaging only serializes recorded results and picks rows in `--chart` "rather than recording a new result". So the promised Year 1 / Year 2 / 24-month grid could not be drawn without reshaping the result. The agent did exactly that at turn 6, once the user insisted (commit cea5151). Nothing in the release told it to carry the preview forward or to flag a departure from it: SKILL.md:49 says the preview file is one "which no check reads", and the reviewer (SKILL.md:79) checks the brief and review rules, not the preview. Reply 5 listed chart 2 as "(bar)" without saying it broke what reply 3 promised, and msg 6 had to ask for the table again.

**"First observed" half (does not hold as stated).** At preview time the brief did not hold a "never new" rule. Line 58 at commits 3327f4c, 24077a2 and 0bac0d4 (line 62 now) reads: "so 'new' means first observed, not first ever". That explicitly allows "new". The preview's "new 2010 customers", with the limitations note that '"new" means first seen since Dec 2009', matches the brief, so a preview-against-brief check would not have caught it. The real slip came earlier, at scoping. The brief template's Audience section has a slot for "the terms they use", but the agent recorded msg 2's "Describe these as first observed purchases" as a definition instead. That is the agent reading the instruction loosely. The preview then did its job: msg 4 caught the wording, the agent added "first observed ... never new" at brief line 32 and as review rules, and the draft used "first observed".

**Overstated claim.** "Nothing records what was agreed at the preview" is wrong for this run, because the preview file recorded the table. What is true is that no later step or check reads that file.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-package/SKILL.md:49: the preview goes to `.preview/headlines.md`, "which no check reads".
- package-contract.md:19: the preview is "not inventoried, checked, or released".
- SKILL.md:79: the reviewer checks the draft against the brief and review rules, not the preview.
- SKILL.md:10: packaging "serializes recorded results"; changed results come only from separately authorized analysis.
- SKILL.md:69: `export` picks columns and filters rows (@first / @where) "rather than recording a new result", with no way to pivot.
- package-format/deck-rules.md:50: the Table form takes about six numbers or a two-way grid.
- awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/brief.md:17: the Audience section records "the terms they use", so the release did offer a place for the first-observed wording that the agent did not use.
- The agent did write "(chart: table, components by year)" in retail-B's draft `.preview/headlines.md` line 10, which the turn-5 draft did not follow.
verdicts.narrowed: Nothing after the headline preview reads it again. The release says `.preview/headlines.md` is read by no check, and the review checks only the brief and review rules. So a draft can drop a chart form agreed at the preview without saying so. In retail-B the preview recorded "chart: table, components by year" for slide 3. The draft instead charted only the 24-month rows as a horizontal bar, and the report never said it had changed. The reason: `export` can filter rows but cannot pivot the long-form reconciliation result into the Year 1 / Year 2 / 24-month grid, and packaging may not reshape results. Reshaping and rerunning the result took a correction round. The "first observed" half does not hold as stated. At preview time the brief allowed "new" to mean first observed, so the preview matched the brief. The agent lost the wording earlier, when it recorded the user's msg-2 instruction as a definition. The preview then caught it as designed, and the agreed wording carried into the draft.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding has two halves. The wording half does not survive checking. The chart half does, in a narrower form.

Wording half ("preview dropped 'first observed' though the brief recorded it"): unsupported.
- When the preview was written (reply 3, commits 3327f4c through 0bac0d4), brief.md defined first observed purchase and added: 'so "new" means first observed, not first ever.' That line allows "new" as shorthand for first observed. It does not forbid "new".
- The preview followed that line. Headline 5 said "new 2010 customers", and the Limitations row explained '"new" means first seen since Dec 2009'.
- The slip happened at scoping. The agent turned the user's msg 2 request ("Describe these as first observed purchases") into a definition that allowed "new". This happened once and was the agent's interpretation.
- The headline preview did its job: the user caught the wording in msg 4.
- The agent then recorded it in the brief's Audience section. Line 32, added in commit 9650661, reads: "first observed" customers, never "new". awb-package SKILL.md line 30 names the Audience section as the place for the audience's terms, and review.md has the reviewer read the brief.
- The draft carried the wording. The reply 5 findings.md has no "new customers", and neither does released 001.
- So "Nothing records what was agreed at the preview" is false for wording. The release's mechanism (Audience terms in the brief, which the reviewer reads) worked, and review rules were added later as well.

Chart half: holds, narrowly.
- In reply 3 the agent promised a Slide 3 table with Year 1, Year 2 and 24-month columns. Its own preview file records "(chart: table, components by year)".
- The reply 5 draft drew "Chart 2. Horizontal bar: net revenue by component over the 24 months". The export call shows `revenue-reconciliation:component,net_revenue@where=period=24 months`.
- The user had to ask for the table again in msg 6. The agent reshaped the result in reply 6 (commit cea5151).

Release causes:
1. The preview is unchecked by design. SKILL.md line 49 and package-contract.md line 19 say no check reads or releases .preview/headlines.md. The preview's documented scope is headlines and figures only. No instruction says that chart forms or layouts shown or promised at the preview must carry into the chart specifications. The reviewer checks against the brief and review rules only, and the brief records no chart forms.
2. The release made the agreed table hard to produce, a plausible but unconfirmed cause. The recorded result was in long format (period, component, net_revenue). The `--chart` grammar (helpers.md line 52) only selects columns and rows (`@first`, `@where`) and cannot pivot to a Year 1 / Year 2 / 24-month grid. SKILL.md lines 10 and 69 say packaging only serializes recorded results, changes to results need separately authorized analysis, and row selection is preferred over recording a new result. So the agreed table could not be built inside packaging without changing a result. Nothing tells the agent to raise that conflict with the user. It quietly picked a chart the existing result could feed. The slide 7 change from table to bar, from the same pass, fits with deck-rules form criteria overriding the preview notes.

Limits on this half:
- The agent could still have shown all three periods, as a clustered bar with a period series or a long table. Dropping Year 1 and Year 2 was its own choice. The agent's notes give no reason for the swap, so cause 2 is inferred.
- The agent did list "(bar)" in its reply 5 chart list. That met the reporting step, but the change was not flagged.
- It happened once, in one run. The correction rode along in msg 6 with other decisions the user had to make anyway, so minor severity is right.
verdicts.release_evidence:
Release files:
- awb-package/SKILL.md line 49: preview-and-wait writes "the title slide and every slide headline" to `.preview/headlines.md`, "which no check reads and no release copies". The scope is headlines and figures, not chart forms.
- awb-package/references/package-contract.md line 19: ".preview/headlines.md ... not inventoried, checked, or released".
- awb-package/references/review.md lines 18 to 28: the reviewer checks the draft against brief.md and review-rules.md. It never reads the preview or anything promised in chat.
- awb-package/SKILL.md lines 10 and 69: "Packaging serializes recorded results ... changed results come only from separately authorized analysis"; select rows in the `--chart` "rather than recording a new result".
- awb-package/references/helpers.md line 52 (and package-contract.md line 71): the `--chart` grammar is closed, only `@first` and `@where` row selection, with no pivot.
- awb-package/SKILL.md line 30: audience terms go in the brief's Audience section. This is the mechanism that did carry the wording.

Run evidence (retail-B):
- The brief at the preview commits (3327f4c, 24077a2, 0bac0d4), line 58 (line 62 now): 'so "new" means first observed, not first ever'. The "never new" wording rule appears only from 9650661, at line 32.
- The preview file records "(chart: table, components by year)".
- relay/agent-005.jsonl: export `revenue-reconciliation:component,net_revenue@where=period=24 months`; findings.md "Chart 2. Horizontal bar ... over the 24 months".
- results/revenue-reconciliation.csv at 24077a2 is in long format (period, component, ...).
- Commit cea5151 reshapes it to a wide table after msg 6.
- The reply 5 draft and released 001 findings.md contain no "new customers".
verdicts.narrowed:
Only presentation choices made at the headline preview are dropped. The 'first observed' wording does not belong in this finding. The brief at preview time explicitly allowed "new" to mean first observed. After the user corrected it in msg 4, the wording was recorded in the brief's Audience section and carried into the draft.

The chart part holds. The reply 3 preview promised a Year 1 / Year 2 / 24-month reconciliation table, and the agent's own .preview/headlines.md recorded it as "chart: table, components by year". The draft drew a 24-month horizontal bar instead, which cost the user a correction in msg 6.

The release has no step that carries chart forms agreed at the preview into the chart specifications or checks them there. By design, no check or reviewer reads .preview/headlines.md.

It also makes the swap likely. The agreed grid needed the long-format reconciliation result pivoted. Export's closed `--chart` grammar cannot pivot, and packaging treats any change to a result as separately authorized analysis. No instruction tells the agent to raise that conflict with the user, so it quietly picked a chart the recorded result could feed.

One occurrence, minor.

consolidated.title: Weekday comparisons are not checked for calendar events
consolidated.description: taxi-A's first Q1 answer reported a July Thursday decline without checking whether July 4, a Thursday, explained it; the user raised it. The July Thursday average was 99,947 with July 4 and 113,478 without. Nothing in the analysis guidance prompts a calendar check when weekday averages are compared.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: taxi-A-14: reply 4 ('Thursday–Saturday declined'), msg 5 item 3, reply 5.

verdicts.reasoning:
The evidence matches the finding. In taxi-A, Codex reply 4 reported the July Thursday average as 103,961 to 99,947 and said "Monday–Wednesday increased; Thursday–Saturday declined" without mentioning holidays. The persona's message 5 item 3 then pointed out that July 4, 2024 was a Thursday. Reply 5 recomputed: 99,947 with July 4, 113,478 without, so the -3.86% change becomes +9.15%. agent-notes.md:58 confirms the arithmetic (59,353 on July 4; the other Thursdays had 113,941, 116,303 and 110,189).

I checked each harness explanation and none holds up:
(1) The persona did not front-load the question. taxi-A/human/BRIEF.md and kit/personas say nothing about holidays or calendars. The persona's notes.md:29 shows it spotted the gap on its own: "agent didn't mention holidays. Asked." That is a sharp user catching a real miss. A less careful user would have passed the misleading weekday comparison to a non-technical board, so the persona's catch, if anything, understates the impact.
(2) The Codex run was not degraded. The agent config is model gpt-6.1-sol with model_reasoning_effort = "high".
(3) Running non-interactively, the sandbox, auto-approved MCP tools and the simulated home all affect tool access, not analytical judgment. The agent computed the weekday table itself and even "normalized calendar exposure" (counts per occurrence of each weekday). What it never did was check calendar events.
(4) The study disclosure says "Work exactly as you normally would." That would not suppress a holiday check.
(5) Codex as the agent is a supported, normal host for this release, so real Codex users would hit the same gap.

The release side checks out. A search of the release for holiday, calendar, weekday or day-of-week guidance finds nothing relevant. workbench-guides/analysis.md asks for period-coverage counts and suggests recording questions "such as whether a dip is seasonal", but nothing prompts a check for calendar events when comparing weekday averages. The miss is also wider than July 4: taxi-A never mentioned that January 2024 had two holiday Mondays (New Year's Day and MLK Day), which inflate July's reported Monday increase.

The finding needs a qualifier. The miss depends on the model: in taxi-B, the Claude agent raised holidays without being asked (transcript line 104 names "two Monday holidays in January, July 4 (a Thursday) in July", and it carried a caveat that holidays are not adjusted for). So the model's judgment is the immediate cause. The release's part is a missing safeguard, not misleading guidance. Once asked, the Codex agent handled the question quickly and correctly. Minor severity is right.
verdicts.release_evidence: The release has no guidance on holiday or calendar events. A grep for holiday/calendar/weekday/day-of-week/confound across release/analytics-workbench-skills returns only unrelated hits: awb_draft.py regex tokens, a DuckDB pragma list, and reading-the-scan.md's "seasonal lows" note for low-period row counts. awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md requires period-coverage counts ("count the periods each entity in scope has data for") and gives "whether a dip is seasonal" as an example of a question to record. It never prompts a check for holidays or calendar events when weekday averages are compared. The low-periods scan flags only periods under half the median, and July 4 (59,353 trips against roughly 100k) would not reach that threshold.
verdicts.narrowed: A Codex agent following the release reported weekday-average changes between January and July without checking holidays. It missed July 4 (a Thursday, which turns -3.86% into +9.15%) and also never mentioned January's two holiday Mondays. Nothing in the release's analysis guidance prompts a calendar-event check when weekdays are compared. The miss depends on the model: taxi-B's Claude agent flagged both months' holidays without being asked. The release's role is a missing safeguard, not a defect that caused the error, and the agent fixed the comparison correctly once the user asked.

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence matches the finding. In taxi-A reply 4 (transcript line 163), July Thursday is shown as 99,947 against 103,961 for January, and line 168 says "Thursday–Saturday declined" with no holiday check. In message 5 item 3 (line 241) the user brings up July 4. Reply 5 (lines 252 and 298–306) then gives 99,947 with July 4 included and 113,478 without it, which reverses the comparison. The agent fixed this in a single turn, and the released findings.md has the July 4 caveat.

The release does not cause this. A search of every shipped file for holiday, calendar or weekday guidance found nothing that tells the agent to skip such checks or that would push it toward the mistake. The gap is missing domain guidance, and the agent failed to apply knowledge it already had:
(1) The taxi-A Codex agent wrote in its own brief during scoping (agent-002/003/004 logs) that "Weather, holidays, travel demand, taxi supply and trip mix remain uncontrolled". It knew holidays could confound the comparison and still did not check July 4 when Thursday fell.
(2) In taxi-B, a Claude agent on the same release brought up the holidays itself in reply 2 (line 104): two Monday holidays in January and July 4, a Thursday, in July. It repeated this as a caveat in later replies. The user there had mentioned weekday mix, but not holidays.
(3) Day-of-week analysis was in scope in all six runs, but only taxi-A showed this lapse.
(4) The guidance taxi-A read in reply 4 already asks for some of this in general terms. analysis.md says "Record a question the analysis raises, such as whether a dip is seasonal". awb-explore asks for a follow-up on each candidate explanation the question turns on.
