Nothing groups related columns, accounts for entity heterogeneity or caps the count. On a wide OWID-style panel covering tiny states up to World and continent aggregates since 1850, almost every numeric column trips one or both tests. The "not read" line comes from resolve_settings (lines 127-131). It lists every [parameters] key except the start/end fallbacks. Yet awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml makes [parameters] the home of run.py's named query parameters. So any investigation that defines run.py parameters before exploring will see them listed, including keys like top_n that could never scope a scan.

The release softens this but does not prevent it. The summary is capped at TABLE_ROWS. SKILL.md step 3 asks for a disposition only for printed anomalies. reading-the-scan.md admits that "Heavy tails are common in amounts and durations". SKILL.md step 3 also tells the agent to check whether an unread settings key changes the population, so that line is intended as a prompt rather than an error. A real user on a normal host who runs awb-explore on a wide panel gets the same mechanical output, and the harness has no part in it. The agent did nothing wrong. It included aggregates on purpose, because its questions need World and EU-27, and the 1850-2024 period matches Q-004.

Impact is low. The agent was not misled. It wrote off the generic scan as low-signal and answered the coverage question with targeted saved queries. Minor severity is right.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-explore/scripts/eda_scan.py:578-579 (high-nulls for any column at 20% null or more); :592-595 (extreme-values whenever beyond_3_iqr > 0, every numeric column, route "investigation"); :990-995 (prints 15 rows plus "N more anomalies"); :127-131 (resolve_settings marks every [parameters] key except the start/end fallbacks as unused); :935 (prints "settings keys not read by the scan"); awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml (makes [parameters] the place for run.py query parameters); awb-explore/SKILL.md step 3 (unread key as a scope check; disposition every printed anomaly); awb-explore/references/reading-the-scan.md (extreme-values: "Heavy tails are common"). Run evidence: co2-B/relay/agent-002.jsonl eda-scan result; co2-B/project/investigations/co2-emissions-change/exploration/eda/owid_co2.json (142 anomalies: 74 extreme-values, 57 high-nulls; date_column year, integer_years true); co2-B/feedback/agent-notes.md turn 2.
verdicts.narrowed: The finding holds as stated, with two qualifications. (1) The flood comes from per-column mechanical thresholds: one or more values beyond 3 IQR, or 20% null or more. Those two kinds make up 131 of the 142 anomalies on an 80-column panel. The printed summary shows only 15 rows, and the harm is lost signal, not wrong results: the agent set the scan aside and answered coverage with targeted queries. (2) The "not read by the scan" line is meant as a scope check (SKILL.md step 3). The problem is that it lists run.py-only [parameters] keys such as top_n and coal_min_co2_mt alongside keys that could matter. That is noise, not a bug.

consolidated.title: Small helper output quirks
consolidated.description: The rescan's compact output printed 'issues: []' while listing issue deltas. profile showed price as float64, though the published schema is DECIMAL(18,6).
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-38: reply 3; agent-notes Turn 3.

verdicts.reasoning:
I read the raw tool results in relay/agent-003.jsonl (turn 3, the turn behind reply 3). Both quirks are there word for word, and both come from release code. The simulation harness did not shape either one.

1. Rescan. The `awb/data clean-scan retail_transactions --name retail-intake --rescan` call returned `delta.issues` with 13 entries, S1-S13: twelve "unchanged" and S6 "resolved". In the same output the top-level field was `"issues":[]`. None of those issues had been recorded yet, because clean-record ran afterwards. The cause is in release awb-clean/scripts/scan_dataset.py, summary(), lines 811-821. On a rescan, `open_issues` is filtered down to keys whose delta change is "new", so the top-level `issues` field shows only new unrecorded issues. The help text the agent read in that same turn says something different: "Stdout lists at most 25 unrecorded issues." SKILL.md and references/checks.md never mention the new-only filter either. So `issues: []` printed next to 12 open, unrecorded baseline issues contradicts the tool's own documentation.

2. Profile. The `awb/read profile retail_transactions` call printed `price | float64`. The project's publication SQL casts price to DECIMAL(18,6), datasets.toml declares that type, and the scan file records it. In release awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py, cli_profile() calls `profile(relation.df())` and prints `str(series.dtype)` under a column headed "type". DuckDB's `.df()` always turns DECIMAL into float64, whatever the host or version. The command's help line says it will "print each column's type". What it actually shows is the pandas dtype, not the SQL type.

How I ruled out harness causes:
- Both outputs are deterministic results of release helpers, relayed unchanged by the release's own awb MCP server; the "exit status 0" trailer is the release's own MCP format.
- The approver MCP, the Codex sandbox, non-interactive codex exec, the simulated home, the relay, the persona and the study disclosure could not change what these helpers print.
- The sandbox did cause the separate here-doc and cache failures in turn 3, but those are unrelated to these outputs.
- The same call on any interactive host would print the same thing.

Severity: minor is right. The agent was not misled into a wrong action. It used exact SQL and CSV decimals for the code audit, and clean-record accepted the baseline IDs.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- **Rescan filter:** release/analytics-workbench-skills/awb-clean/scripts/scan_dataset.py summary(), lines 819-821: `new = {d["key"] for d in delta["issues"] if d["change"] == "new"}` / `open_issues = [i for i in open_issues if i["key"] in new]` / `out["issues"] = [_compact(i) for i in open_issues[:limit]]`.
- **Help text contradicts it:** the same file's docstring, which is the clean-scan help the agent read, says "Stdout lists at most 25 unrecorded issues".
- **Not documented elsewhere:** SKILL.md line 49 says only that stdout "reports each issue's before and after counts".
- **Profile dtype:** release/analytics-workbench-skills/awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py. cli_profile() calls `result = profile(relation.df())`, and profile() stores `"dtype": str(series.dtype)`, which is printed under the header "type".
- **CLI help line:** awb_cli.py describes profile as "print each column's type".
- **Observed output:** in relay/agent-003.jsonl the rescan result has `"issues":[]` alongside 13 delta entries, and the profile result has `| price | float64 |`.
- **Declared type:** project/src/preparation/retail_transactions.sql:20 has `CAST(Price AS DECIMAL(18,6))`, and foundation/datasets.toml declares price as "DECIMAL(18,6)".
verdicts.narrowed:
Two minor documentation and labelling defects in the helpers:
- **Rescan output:** on a rescan, the compact `issues` field lists only new unrecorded issues, by design. Its help text says it lists unrecorded issues, so `issues: []` appears beside baseline issues that are still unrecorded and reads as contradictory.
- **Profile output:** the "type" column shows the pandas dtype from DuckDB's `.df()`, not the SQL type, so a DECIMAL(18,6) column appears as float64.

Neither defect caused a wrong result in this run.

verdicts.reasoning:
Both quirks show up in the run log, and both come from shipped helper code that behaves the same on any host. Neither one is caused by the harness.

(1) The empty issues list after a rescan. In retail-A relay/agent-003.jsonl, the `clean-scan ... --rescan` result shows "delta":{"issues":[13 lines: S1..S13, 12 unchanged and S6 resolved]} next to a top-level "issues":[]. None of the 13 issues was recorded at that point, because clean-record ran later. The cause is `summary()` in awb-clean/scripts/scan_dataset.py. On a rescan, line 820 (`open_issues = [i for i in open_issues if i["key"] in new]`) cuts the top-level `issues` down to issues that are both new and unrecorded. In this run there were no new issues, so the list came out empty. The docs never describe this change in meaning. awb-clean/SKILL.md line 22 and the script's docstring both say stdout "lists up to 25 unrecorded issues". Step 4 (Confirm) mentions only the before and after counts. So the release produces an empty issues list while 12 unrecorded baseline issues are still open, and no instruction warns about it.

(2) price shown as float64. The `profile` result in the same log reports `price | float64`. The project declares price as DECIMAL(18,6) in foundation/datasets.toml and in src/preparation/retail_transactions.sql. The cause is `cli_profile` in awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py. Line 300 converts the DuckDB relation to pandas with `profile(relation.df())`, which turns DECIMAL into float64. Line 321 then prints the pandas dtype under a column headed "type". The CLI help (awb_cli.py line 39) promises "each column's type". awb-init/references/validation.md documents only the Python `dtype` field and gives no warning that the CLI prints pandas dtypes instead of SQL types.

Impact is minor. The agent noticed both quirks and worked around them: it used exact SQL and CSV decimals, and clean-record recorded the baseline IDs without trouble. The output reaches the agent, not the end user, so a user would only be affected if an agent misread it. Even so, the release causes both behaviours and documents neither. One correction to the cited evidence: retail-A/feedback/findings.json has only retail-A-01 to retail-A-19, so the ID retail-A-38 does not exist there. The facts behind it are confirmed directly in agent-notes Turn 3 (lines 46 and 48) and in the agent-003.jsonl tool results.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-clean/scripts/scan_dataset.py summary(): line 820 `open_issues = [i for i in open_issues if i["key"] in new]` before `out["issues"] = ...` (line 821), so on a rescan the list holds only new unrecorded issues. Neither awb-clean/SKILL.md line 22 ("lists up to 25 unrecorded issues"), the step 4 Confirm text, nor the script docstring mentions this. awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py cli_profile(): line 300 `result = profile(relation.df())` (DuckDB DECIMAL becomes pandas float64) and line 321 prints `["column", "type", ...]` filled with column["dtype"]. awb_cli.py line 39 describes the output as "each column's type". Run evidence: retail-A/relay/agent-003.jsonl rescan result `"delta":{"rows":[1067371,1067371],"issues":["S1 ... unchanged", ..., "S6 whitespace:description: 213035 -> 0 resolved", ...]},"issues":[]`, and the profile result row `| price | float64 | 0.0 | 2807 |`. The project's datasets.toml and retail_transactions.sql declare price DECIMAL(18,6).
verdicts.narrowed: Both quirks are agent-facing and cost nothing in this run. (1) On --rescan, scan_dataset.py's compact stdout cuts the top-level `issues` to new unrecorded issues only, and nothing documents that. So `issues: []` appears while all unchanged baseline issues are still unrecorded. (2) `awb profile` prints pandas dtypes after a `.df()` conversion under a column labelled "type", so DuckDB DECIMAL(18,6) columns show as float64. No wrong result or user-visible error followed, and the agent worked around both.

consolidated.title: The review receipt accepted a report missing its problems and errors lines
consolidated.description: co2-A's full review report left out the 'problems' and 'errors' lines that review.md's brief requires, and review-receipt record accepted it as a valid report.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: possibly: review-receipt record, added by #96 (issue #84), does not check the report's shape.
consolidated.evidence: co2-A-27: agent-006 review-receipt record stdin (only a narrative line and a 'review:' line); review.md Brief step 4.

verdicts.reasoning:
The facts in the finding check out, and nothing in the harness caused them.

1. The omission came from the reviewer itself. The full-review subagent ran as a Codex `spawn_agent` fork, `fork_turns: "all"`, in rollout `agent-home/.codex/sessions/2026/10/17/rollout-...01a149ae...jsonl`. It first read the installed review.md, which matches the release copy byte for byte. It then ran `awb/read review-rules` and got back `{"rules_file": "none recorded", "rules": [], "problems": [], "errors": []}` with exit 0. Its final answer was only two lines: the `narrative ... methodology-note.md:27 ...` line and `review: 0 violations (0 error), 1 narrative problems, 0 command problems`.

2. Neither the relay nor the parent changed the report. In the parent rollout at 11:46:41, the agent passed that exact text as stdin to `review-receipt record --kind full --report -`. The record call completed without refusal.

3. The acceptance is release code working as written. The installed `src/packaging/draft.py` is identical to the release's `awb_draft.py`. Its `review_summary` (line 4617) refuses a report only when:
   - the last line does not parse;
   - the kind does not match;
   - errors exceed violations;
   - a clean report carries acceptances; or
   - the body has more violation or narrative rows than the last line counts.
   It never checks for the `problems`/`errors` lines that Brief step 4 requires, or for per-rule lines. The `record_review` docstring at line 4691 says this is intended: "a report that passes ... is not checked, since the Brief fixes its words."

4. No harness factor applies:
   - Codex multi-agent forking behaves the same in an interactive Codex session, and the release names Codex as a supported host.
   - The sandbox, MCP auto-approval, the simulated home, personas and the study note have nothing to do with what the reviewer wrote or what the record call validates.

5. The pattern is not tied to Codex. Claude-agent runs also recorded reports with no problems/errors lines, and the receipt accepted them: co2-B agent-004/005/006 and taxi-B agent-005/006. Other runs did include `problems: []` / `errors: []`, as did co2-A's own scoped reviews.

The impact here is close to nothing:
- Both omitted lists were empty, so no information was lost.
- The last line's `0 command problems` was correct.
- `passed` was computed correctly as False (one unaccepted narrative problem).
- The fix went through a scoped review that came back clean.

The Brief also invites the omission. "The command's `problems` and `errors` verbatim" reads naturally as having nothing to copy when both lists are empty.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- `awb-package/references/review.md`, Brief step 4, third bullet (line 32): "the command's `problems` and `errors` verbatim, or `command failed` with its output when it did not run".
- `awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py`:
  - `review_summary` (line 4617) parses only the last line, plus counts of `R-... violation` rows (`_VIOLATION_ROW`, line 4510) and `narrative` rows (`_NARRATIVE_ROW`, line 4511). It never looks for `problems` or `errors` lines, and never matches command-problem rows against the count of `<c> command problems`.
  - The `record_review` docstring (line 4691) says a report that passes is "not checked, since the Brief fixes its words".
- The installed copy (`co2-A/project/src/packaging/draft.py`) is identical to the release file.
- Subagent rollout `co2-A/agent-home/.codex/sessions/2026/10/17/rollout-2026-10-17T07-45-39-01a149ae-...jsonl`: the `review-rules` output had empty problems/errors, and the final message was only the narrative line and the summary line.
- Parent rollout at 11:46:41: the parent recorded that text verbatim, and the record completed.
verdicts.narrowed: `review-receipt record` checks a report's body only for an undercount of its own violation and narrative rows. It does not require the Brief step 4 lines, meaning the command's `problems`/`errors` lines (and per-rule lines). Reviewers on both Codex and Claude Code often leave out the problems/errors lines when both lists are empty, and the receipt records those reports anyway. In co2-A both lists were empty, so nothing was lost, and `passed` was computed correctly. The real gap is hypothetical: a report that drops non-empty `problems`/`errors` and still counts `0 command problems` would also be accepted. That would let a review pass even though a command problem went unreported.

verdicts.reasoning:
The cited evidence holds. In co2-A, the full reviewer (Codex subagent "Faraday", rollout 01a149ae) read review.md with cat. It then ran review-rules through awb/read and got {"rules_file": "none recorded", "rules": [], "problems": [], "errors": []} with exit 0. Its final message had only two lines: one narrative line and "review: 0 violations (0 error), 1 narrative problems, 0 command problems". agent-006 passed that text unchanged as stdin to review-receipt record --kind full (relay agent-006.jsonl; review-reports/agent-006-record01.txt), and record accepted it.

Release cause, part 1 (validator): review.md Brief step 4 requires "the command's `problems` and `errors` verbatim". The record path in awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py never checks for those lines. review_summary reads only the last non-blank line against _SUMMARY, then checks that the kind matches, that errors <= violations, and that the body's violation and narrative rows do not outnumber the counts. No check looks for `problems:`/`errors:` lines, and record never compares the report with the review-rules output. review.md's "After the review" describes record's refusals in the same narrow terms (no start, or an input changed), so acceptance is the shipped behaviour.

Release cause, part 2 (instruction wording): this was not one agent ignoring a clear instruction once. Across all six runs, 11 of 23 recorded reports omit the lines: co2-A 1 of 3, taxi-B 4 of 4, co2-B 5 of 5. In co2-B the parent's brief told the Plan reviewer to "follow its **Brief** section exactly" and "Return exactly the report format in Brief step 4". The reviewer still dropped the lines. Both Codex and Claude reviewers read "verbatim" as nothing to write when both lists are empty. Other reviewers wrote "problems: []" / "errors: []", including the two later co2-A reviewers and those in taxi-A, retail-A and retail-B.

Impact is cosmetic. In every review-rules call a reviewer made, the problems and errors lists were empty, and every summary line counted 0 command problems. Pass/fail depends only on the summary line, so leaving the lines out lost nothing and changed no outcome. The only real risk is untested: a reviewer drops non-empty problems and also writes 0 command problems. record would accept that, because it never re-runs or compares with review-rules check.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-package/references/review.md line 32 (Brief step 4): "the command's `problems` and `errors` verbatim, or `command failed` with its output when it did not run". Line 39 ("After the review"): record refuses only when no review was started or an input changed. awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py: review_summary (about lines 4613-4646) parses only the last line with _SUMMARY plus _VIOLATION_ROW/_NARRATIVE_ROW counts. Its docstring lists the refusals: a last line that does not parse, a kind mismatch, more errors than violations, a clean line given acceptances, or a body with more rows than counted. Nothing requires or checks `problems`/`errors` lines. Run evidence: the co2-A Faraday rollout shows review-rules returned empty problems and errors, and the final message has no such lines. review-reports across runs: the lines are missing in co2-A agent-006-record01, all 4 taxi-B reports and all 5 co2-B reports.
verdicts.narrowed: This is a harmless gap in report format, not a defect a user would notice. review-receipt record checks only the report's summary line and its row counts. It never checks for the `problems:`/`errors:` lines that Brief step 4 asks for. Step 4's "verbatim" wording also leaves the empty case unclear, so reviewers of both model families often drop the lines when the command returns empty lists (11 of 23 recorded reports, in co2-A, taxi-B and co2-B). In every observed case the lists were empty and the summary counted 0 command problems, so no information or pass/fail outcome was affected. Two possible fixes: say that empty lists are still written as `problems: []` / `errors: []`, or have record require those lines.

consolidated.title: Hard-coded row counts instead of reconcile()
consolidated.description: co2-B's q1-full-ranking hard-codes its row counts (218/215/3) in settings instead of using a producer that calls reconcile(), which will break if the data is landed again.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: co2-B-41: [results.q1-full-ranking.validation] in settings.toml; the settings template says row counts usually come from a producer through reconcile().

verdicts.reasoning:
I looked for a harness cause and found none.

What happened: in turn 3 (relay/agent-003.jsonl) the Claude agent was inside the awb-package skill when the user asked for "the full ranking tables as supporting datasets". To supply them it added result q1-full-ranking. It wrote the settings with one Bash heredoc that appended a static row_counts step, before = 218, after = 215, excluded = {"no CO2 in start or end year" = 3}. It did not write producers/q1-full-ranking.py. The numbers were copied from the counts that q1-change-since-2000's producer had measured with reconcile(). The evidence for both results shows identical "218 = 215 kept + 3 excluded" details, and the CSV has 215 rows, so the counts are correct today.

The agent knew this was a shortcut. Its private log says it was "brittle if data re-landed; the producer route would be better but heavier" (feedback/agent-notes.md, turn 3). It lists the same point as a deviation in feedback/agent.md, section 4.

Harness factors checked:
- **Non-interactive `claude -p`:** no question needed asking, so this played no part.
- **Codex sandbox, MCP auto-approval, simulated home, relay:** none of them touched the decision. The agent was Claude, it wrote with Bash and ran the result with mcp__awb__run, and the run went through.
- **System prompt and study note:** neither adds time or token pressure. The friction-log note made the agent report the shortcut; it did not cause it.
- **Persona:** the user's request for full tables, bundled with other asks in turn 3, is an ordinary request a real user would make.
- **Turn budget:** 28 turns, no denials, no errors.

The cause is the agent taking a known shortcut. The release lets that shortcut through:
- The settings template says counts come "Usually from a producer, through reconcile()". That is soft wording, and static row_counts in settings are a documented, accepted form.
- `_row_counts()` in src/exploration/validate.py never compares a list-form step's `after` with len(frame). A hand-copied step can therefore never fail.
- The new result was built inside awb-package, which says packaging "serializes" recorded results. The agent never reloaded analysis.md, which says every filtered population should be reconciled with reconcile().

A real user on a normal host could end up with the same stale counts, and the release would not catch them.

Corrections to the finding:
- "Will break if the data is landed again" is wrong. After a re-landing that changed the counts, validation would still pass and would record a stale "reconciled: 218 = 215 kept + 3 excluded" detail. The counts would go stale silently, which is arguably worse than breaking.
- This happened in 1 of 6 runs. Only co2-B has data-dependent static row_counts. The other two runs with a Claude agent (taxi-B, retail-B) and all three runs with a Codex agent used producers.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml lines 38-40: row_counts are listed as a static spec key in settings, with only "Usually from a producer, through reconcile() (see run.py)".
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md line 15: "every filtered population reconciled by `reconcile()` ... as `run.py`'s producer example shows". This guidance exists, but it is not part of the awb-package flow the agent was in.
- awb-init/references/validation.md line 14: a step's `excluded` is checked only for before = after + excluded. There is no comparison with the result's length.
- `_row_counts` in the installed src/exploration/validate.py (project copy, lines 97-131): only an integer form compares with len(frame). List-form steps are checked internally only, so static settings counts always pass.
- awb-package/SKILL.md line 10: "Packaging **serializes** recorded results ... changed results come only from separately authorized analysis". The agent created the new result inside this skill without reloading the analysis guide.
verdicts.narrowed: In co2-B, while it was packaging, the Claude agent added q1-full-ranking with row counts (218/215/3) hand-copied into settings.toml and no producer calling reconcile(). It did this against analysis.md and the settings template's "usually through reconcile()", and logged it as a known shortcut. The counts are correct today. The release's validate() never compares list-form row_counts with the result's row count, so a re-landing that changed the counts would not break the run: it would pass silently and record a stale "reconciled" detail as evidence. Seen in 1 of 6 runs.

verdicts.reasoning:
The observation is accurate, but the release did not cause it. The agent went against a clear instruction it had already read and followed elsewhere in the same run.

1) The evidence holds. co2-B/project/investigations/co2-emissions-change/settings.toml has [results.q1-full-ranking.validation] with row_counts = [{ before = 218, after = 215, excluded = { "no CO2 in start or end year" = 3 } }] and no producers/q1-full-ranking.py. relay/agent-003.jsonl shows the agent appending this table with a heredoc during a turn where it had invoked awb-package for a headline preview. The user had asked for "the full ranking tables as supporting datasets".

2) The release tells agents to do the opposite:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md (copied into the project as workbench-guides/analysis.md) says to specify "plausible counts before and after each filter, with every filtered population reconciled by `reconcile()` ... as `run.py`'s producer example shows".
- The settings.toml template says row_counts come "Usually from a producer, through reconcile() (see run.py)".
- run.py carries a full producer example built on reconcile().

3) The agent knew the right pattern. It read analysis.md in agent-002 and wrote reconcile() producers for q1-change-since-2000, q2 and q5. The q1-change-since-2000 producer and its counts query (q1-change-since-2000-counts.sql) compute exactly the 218/215/3 step for the same population, so a three-line producer would have done it.

4) The agent called this a shortcut itself. feedback/agent-notes.md:58 says "the producer route would be better but heavier", and feedback/agent.md:93 says it is "quicker but brittle".

5) It happened once, in a packaging turn where awb-package says packaging only serializes. That is one deviation from a clear instruction, not repeated ignoring caused by unclear text.

The finding's wording is also slightly off. The counts would not "break" if the data were landed again. awb_validate._row_counts checks only that a list-form step adds up (before == after + excluded) and stays within its ratio bounds. It never compares the step to the frame. So the hard-coded 218/215/3 would keep passing with stale numbers. That gap in the safety net is real, but cross-checking a step against the frame length is not valid in general: a step can count entities or summed orders rather than rows, as run.py's own example does. It is also not what this finding claims.
verdicts.release_evidence:
The release already instructs against this:
- release/analytics-workbench-skills/awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/analysis.md, under "Add a result": "with every filtered population reconciled by `reconcile()`, rows in equal to rows kept plus rows excluded by each rule, as `run.py`'s producer example shows".
- awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/settings.toml, line 40: "Usually from a producer, through reconcile() (see run.py)."
- awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/run.py, lines 71-87: a producer example built on reconcile().
- awb-init/references/validation.md, line 14: "Supply observed counts and justified bounds for each relevant operation."

The release leaves one gap open: awb-init/assets/awb_validate.py, _row_counts (lines 97-132), checks a static list step's internal arithmetic only and never compares it to the frame, so hard-coded counts are accepted.

Run evidence:
- co2-B/relay/agent-002.jsonl: the agent reads analysis.md.
- co2-B/relay/agent-003.jsonl: the agent appends q1-full-ranking with static counts.
- co2-B/project/investigations/co2-emissions-change/producers/q1-change-since-2000.py: the same 218/215/3 step computed through reconcile().
- co2-B/feedback/agent-notes.md:58: the agent's own note admitting the shortcut.
verdicts.narrowed: Once, in a packaging turn, co2-B's agent copied observed counts into a static row_counts step for q1-full-ranking. This went against analysis.md's reconcile() instruction, which the agent followed for its other filtered results. If the data were landed again, the step would not break: it would keep passing validation with stale numbers, because validate() checks only a static step's own arithmetic. This is an agent shortcut, not something the release caused.

consolidated.title: A question only IT could answer, asked without a fallback recommendation
consolidated.description: retail-A asked whether manual and bank postings are customer charges or internal entries, a question only IT could answer, and gave no recommended treatment to fall back on.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-10: reply 3; msg 4; human.md pain point 6; AGENTS.md Conversation ('with your recommendation and the alternative').

verdicts.reasoning:
The evidence supports the finding, and no harness factor explains it.

What happened (retail-A/relay/agent-003.out.md, reply 3): the intake table set the "proposed revenue treatment" for BANK CHARGES to "Review mixed postings" and for M/m to "Review manual entries". The reply then said "neither supports a blanket exclusion yet" and ended with "If you know whether manual and bank postings represent customer charges/credits or internal entries, that will resolve their treatment." It offered no treatment for the analysis to use if the user could not answer. The agent's own intake-review.md (line 23) defines Review as "insufficient evidence for a blanket include or exclude", and line 77 leaves both codes "unresolved until then (Q-012)". In agent-notes.md (line 40) the agent says it chose review over deletion on purpose. It was a judgment call, not a slip under pressure. In human-004 the user had to come up with the fallback herself: exclude from headline revenue, state the amounts in a caveat, and say whether the exclusion changes any answer.

Harness factors checked and rejected:
- **Non-interactive codex exec.** One question at the end of a turn is also normal on an interactive host. It has nothing to do with whether a recommendation is included.
- **Sandbox, auto-approved MCP tools, simulated home.** None of these touch what goes into a reply.
- **Study disclosure.** It asks for a private friction log, which gives no reason to hold back a recommendation.
- **Rules not in context.** The agent ran `cat AGENTS.md` and read awb-clean/SKILL.md in this same turn, so the Conversation rule and the table rule were both loaded.
- **Persona front-loading.** It works against the harness reading. The persona asked outright for the agent's recommendation on non-product revenue (human-002), so the missing fallback was more visible, not caused by the persona.

One part does come from the harness: the "only IT could answer" framing. The persona brief says order-system questions "are for the company's IT team". Even so, a real head of e-commerce plausibly would not know either, and the core defect (no fallback recommendation) stands whether or not the user knows.

Model variance: in retail-B, where Claude was the agent, the agent asked the non-product revenue question during scoping with "I recommend… / The alternative…". So this is one occurrence, from the Codex agent. Codex is a supported host, though, so a real Codex user could hit the same behavior.

Release attribution: the release already requires a recommendation in both places below, so this is mainly the agent not following an existing rule. Still, awb-clean's "Ask when examples or source context leave meaning ambiguous" lets "Review" pass as a proposed treatment. Neither awb-clean nor awb-scope says what to do when the answer may lie with a third party, such as giving a default the work can proceed on. The release leaves room for this behavior, so it is a real but minor product issue.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- **Project AGENTS.md** (awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md:32): "When you need the user, ask in that message for a plain decision, with your recommendation and the alternative".
- **awb-clean/SKILL.md §2 Decide:** "Ask all of these in one message, as a table of issue, observation with count and examples, proposed treatment, and the alternative." It also says "Ask when examples or source context leave meaning ambiguous", with no requirement for a fallback treatment.
- **awb-scope/SKILL.md:44:** "ask the user every open decision they can answer, and the context only they hold". There is no rule for questions whose real answerer is a third party such as IT.
- **README.md:62:** "The agent asks in plain words, with its recommendation and the alternative."
- **Run artifacts (retail-A):**
  - relay/agent-003.jsonl shows `cat AGENTS.md` and the awb-clean SKILL.md read in the same turn.
  - relay/agent-003.out.md: table rows "BANK CHARGES … Review mixed postings" and "M … Review manual entries", plus the closing conditional question.
  - project/investigations/marketing-budget/exploration/intake-review.md lines 23 and 77.
  - feedback/agent-notes.md line 40 (deliberate "need review instead of automatic deletion").
- **Persona:** kit/personas/retail.md routes order-system questions to IT and asks for the agent's recommendation on non-product revenue.
- **Contrast:** retail-B/relay/agent-001.out.md (Claude as agent) gives "I recommend… / The alternative…" for the same revenue question.
verdicts.narrowed: In one run (retail-A, Codex as agent), at the intake checkpoint, the agent proposed "Review" (no treatment) for two ambiguous code groups, M/m and BANK CHARGES (about -£118k signed). It asked what the postings mean without a fallback the analysis could proceed on if the user did not know, so the user had to work out the exclude-plus-caveat treatment herself. The release's AGENTS.md and awb-clean rules already require a recommendation and an alternative, so this is mainly the agent not complying. The release's part is narrower: it does not require a default treatment when a meaning question may only be answerable by someone else (for example IT), and it accepts "ask when ambiguous" without one. The "only IT could answer" framing comes partly from the persona brief, which routes order-system questions to IT.

verdicts.reasoning:
The run evidence is real. In retail-A reply 3 (transcript.md lines 126-150) the intake table gave BANK CHARGES "Review mixed postings" and M/m "Review manual entries" instead of a treatment. The reply then asked, "If you know whether manual and bank postings represent customer charges/credits or internal entries, that will resolve their treatment," and offered no working treatment or alternative. intake-review.md defines "Review" as "insufficient evidence for a blanket include or exclude." In message 4 the user had to make up the fallback herself: exclude the codes from headline revenue, state the amounts and run a sensitivity check. human.md pain point 6 confirms this. The agent also had less excuse than usual. In message 2 the user had explicitly asked for its recommendation on whether these codes belong in revenue (ledger Q-011: "The user requested the analyst's recommendation on their inclusion in revenue"). The agent's reply 2 answer for manual entries was only "Review manual entries individually and quantify ambiguous amounts."

The release does not cause this. It forbids it in three places:
(1) The project AGENTS.md Conversation section (shipped at awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md, identical to the project copy) says: "When you need the user, ask in that message for a plain decision, with your recommendation and the alternative."
(2) awb-clean SKILL.md step 2, which was the skill in use for this pass, covers issues "the user decides" because they change meaning. It says: "Ask all of these in one message, as a table of issue, observation with count and examples, proposed treatment, and the alternative." The agent built that table but entered "Review" as the treatment and left the alternative column out.
(3) README "What you will be asked" promises: "The agent asks in plain words, with its recommendation and the alternative."

This was a single slip in a run where every other question did carry a recommendation, and human.md praises "A recommendation with every question." So the agent did not ignore an instruction repeatedly. retail-B ran the same release on the same data. It put the manual/bank codes inside a recommended treatment ("products only... show postage and the other non-product lines as one separate total") with an explicit alternative, so the release does not reliably produce this behaviour. One possible contributor is awb-clean's plain-words example for cross-sheet duplicates ("Are they two exports of the same rows, or separate stores...?"). It is phrased as a factual question with no recommendation. But it covers a different issue type, and the table rule the agent was following plainly asks for a proposed treatment.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md line 32 (Conversation): "When you need the user, ask in that message for a plain decision, with your recommendation and the alternative; never send them to a skill or instruction file."
- awb-clean/SKILL.md, step 2 Decide: "The user decides every other issue, because each changes meaning: ... Ask all of these in one message, as a table of issue, observation with count and examples, proposed treatment, and the alternative."
- README.md line 62: "The agent asks in plain words, with its recommendation and the alternative."
- Possible minor contributor: awb-clean/SKILL.md cross-sheet duplicates example ("Sheets north and south share 12 rows identical in every column. Are they two exports of the same rows, or separate stores whose rows happen to match?") models a factual question with no recommendation.
- Counter-run: retail-B transcript lines 40-42 handled the same codes with "I recommend" plus "The alternative."
verdicts.narrowed: In retail-A reply 3 alone, the agent marked M/m and BANK CHARGES as "Review" with no proposed treatment and asked a question only IT could answer. That breaks the explicit rules in AGENTS.md (Conversation) and awb-clean step 2, both of which require a proposed treatment and the alternative, so it is agent non-compliance, not something the release causes. The most the release can be blamed for is a small documentation gap. Nothing in awb-clean says to propose a working treatment that still holds when only a third party knows what a code means, and its cross-sheet example question carries no recommendation. The README also does not tell users that "I don't know, recommend something" is an acceptable answer. None of this is shown to have caused the behaviour.

consolidated.title: Retained copy of a public dataset page embeds a third party's email address
consolidated.description: The retained copy of the public UCI dataset page, committed to Git, embeds a third party's email address in its JSON payload.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: retail-A-26: foundation/references/online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html (committed); workbench-guides/data.md.

verdicts.reasoning: The facts hold, but the harness explanation does not. In agent-003 the retail-A agent (Codex) fetched https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/502/online+retail+ii with a plain, unauthenticated urllib GET and wrote the raw bytes to foundation/references/online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html. The email (<email>, under "users" in an edit-history record) is in the hydration JSON that UCI's own public page serves to any visitor. The agent kept the page because the release asks it to: workbench-guides/data.md says to "Keep each data dictionary, manual, codebook, or schema export that an assessment ... relies on under foundation/references/<source-id>/", and awb-status flags documentation_without_reference. The user (persona) supplied only the ZIP URL, never the dataset page, and never asked for documentation. README says "Commits: on request". The agent itself recommended committing the source documentation (agent-003.out.md), and the user replied "Go ahead and commit" (agent-004.in.md), which is ordinary user behavior. Nothing here depends on the Codex sandbox, codex exec, auto-approved MCP, the simulated home, the relay or the study disclosure. retail-B, where Claude was the agent, independently saved and committed the same page with the same email (commit 3327f4c). The behavior therefore carries across agent models and would happen on a normal interactive host. On an interactive host the network-fetch approval would not reveal the page contents, so it would not change the outcome. The only harness contributions are (a) the referee's identity audit, which is what made a public address look like a leak, and (b) presenting a public UCI dataset as "our transaction export". Neither caused the file to exist. Real users analyzing public datasets would get the same result. The finding still overstates the problem, though. The address is already published by the source site to every visitor. The release's instruction is to keep a faithful copy of third-party documentation, and changing the copy would weaken its value as provenance. No user-identifying or confidential data leaked. Calling this a release-caused privacy defect is not supported. The referee's own tag (retail-A-19, harness) is also wrong on the cause. The agent was not "asked to document" the page by the user. The release's retention rule produced it.
verdicts.release_evidence: awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md, Assess and acquire: keep each data dictionary, manual, codebook or schema export the assessment relies on under foundation/references/<source-id>/, and commit it or suggest committing it. The release gives no guidance on what form a retained web page should take (rendered text, PDF or raw HTML) and none on incidental personal data in third-party material. The only exclusion is material "whose license or confidentiality bars committing it". CHANGELOG.md line 264 introduces foundation/references/ and awb-status sources.documentation_without_reference. Run evidence: retail-A/relay/agent-003.jsonl (urllib fetch writing the raw page bytes); agent-003.out.md (agent recommends committing the source documentation); agent-004.in.md (user: "Go ahead and commit"); commit 9096f84. Cross-check: retail-B/project/foundation/references/uci-online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html, also committed (3327f4c) and containing the same address.
verdicts.narrowed: Narrower product observation, a quality issue rather than a privacy one: when the documentation is a web page, the data guide's retention rule leads both Codex and Claude agents to commit the raw HTML of a JavaScript-rendered dataset page. That is 85 KB of hydration JSON, carrying whatever the site embeds (here the UCI editor's already-public email), when a readable extract or PDF of the variable descriptions would serve better. The release says nothing about the form a retained web page should take. This is not a harness artifact, and it is not a privacy defect the release caused.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding is accurate. In retail-A the file project/foundation/references/online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html is tracked in Git (git ls-files lists it; it was added in commit 9096f84). Its embedded Next.js/tRPC JSON payload holds UCI's edit-history record, which contains "users":{"firstName":"<third-party>","lastName":"<third-party>","user":"<email>"}. That email appears twice.

The release is what drives this. Line 11 of awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md tells the agent to keep each data dictionary, manual, codebook or schema export that an assessment relies on under foundation/references/<source-id>/, and to commit it or suggest committing it. foundation/sources.md then requires a `reference:` link to that kept copy, and awb-status counts a missing one as a limitation. The only exception in the release is material whose license or confidentiality bars committing it. The release never says how to capture a web page (rendered text or a PDF versus raw HTML carrying the site's app-state payload). It also never says to check a retained document for personal data before committing it. A search of the shipped files for personal data, PII, email or privacy finds nothing else.

The agent's own behaviour matches: in relay agent-003, right after reading data.md, the Codex agent saved the page by fetching it with urlopen and writing the bytes to foundation/references/online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html. Retail-B, where Claude was the agent, did the same thing independently: references/uci-online-retail-ii/uci-dataset-page.html is committed in 3327f4c and contains the same email. Two agents from different model families following the same guide both produced this result, so it is not one agent's quirk. Any real user analysing a UCI dataset with this release would get the same outcome.

The referee tagged retail-A-19 as harness on the grounds that "the agent was asked to document" the page. That is not correct: the user never asked for the page to be kept. The workbench guide asked for it. The brief does supply the public URL, so the choice of dataset comes from the harness, but public UCI datasets are a normal real-world input.

Two caveats keep the severity minor or lower. First, the email is already published by UCI on its own public page, so the harm is only that it gets republished if the project repo is shared. Second, saving raw HTML rather than an extracted copy was the agent's choice, although the release offers no alternative.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- awb-init/assets/workbench/workbench-guides/data.md:11 requires keeping and committing the documentation an assessment relies on, with an exception only for license or confidentiality. It says nothing on how to capture a web page or on personal data in documents.
- awb-init/assets/workbench/foundation/sources.md:16-22 requires a `reference:` link to the kept copy.
- README.md:193 says third-party documentation is kept under foundation/references/<source-id>/.
- A search of the release finds no privacy or PII guidance anywhere else.
- Run evidence: in retail-A relay agent-003 the agent read data.md, then urlopen'd https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/502/online+retail+ii and wrote the raw bytes to uci-dataset-page.html. The file is tracked in commit 9096f84 and contains <email> twice, in the users object of the edits JSON.
- Retail-B (Claude agent) did the same and committed it in 3327f4c.
verdicts.narrowed: The data guide requires keeping and committing the third-party documentation a source assessment relies on. It says nothing on how to capture a web page or on checking for personal data. Agents therefore save the raw HTML of a dataset page, which brings along whatever app-state JSON the site embeds. Both retail runs (retail-A with Codex, retail-B with Claude) committed the UCI page with an editor's name and email from UCI's edit-history payload. That data is already public on UCI's site, so the harm is only republication if the repo is shared: minor at most.

consolidated.title: 'Changed on disk' notifications re-show whole files
consolidated.description: retail-B's agent reported repeated Claude Code 'changed on disk' notifications that re-showed whole files whenever helpers rewrote files it had read, which cost tokens.
consolidated.caused_by_fix: no
consolidated.evidence: retail-B-40: agent.md section 5; the notifications are not visible in the stream-json logs, so this cannot be verified.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding says the notifications cannot be verified. They can: they are in the Claude session transcript, not in the stream-json logs. The relay runs claude with the real HOME, so the transcript is at ~/.claude/projects/-private-tmp-...-sims-retail-B-project/ebd9398b-6924-4c3b-ab8a-63483f4849a2.jsonl. That file holds 32 `edited_text_file` attachments, Claude Code's own "file changed on disk" reminder, with 93,009 characters of snippets in total. Three harness causes account for almost all of the cost.

1. **One fresh process per relay turn.** The relay starts a new `claude -p --resume <id>` for every turn (agent-002.err through agent-008.err). 26 of the 32 attachments, 84,815 characters or 91%, fire at the exact instant a resumed process starts (11:27:55, 11:34:03, 11:36:34, 11:48:35, 11:53:34, 11:55:23). Several are byte-identical repeats of a reminder already shown:
   - state.md: the same snippet (md5 612ac860) at entry 416, mid-turn, and again at entry 450 on resume.
   - agent-notes.md: the same snippet (a10513ce) at entries 436 and 451.
   - methodology-note.md: the same snippet (b68ec9ec) at entries 1158, 1322 and 1420, across three resumes.
   - brief.md: an empty snippet re-sent on five resumes.

   A resumed process rebuilds its record of which files it has read and re-notifies every file changed since then. Inside one process, each change is shown only once. In this run, no file is re-shown twice within the same process; the only identical repeats come right after a restart. The "repeated" part of the complaint is therefore a product of the per-turn resume. An interactive session is one long-lived process and would not do this.

2. **The study's own notes file.** 47,915 characters, 52% of the total and the largest snippets (up to 8,118 characters, the first ~60 lines plus a "[N lines truncated]" marker), come from feedback/agent-notes.md. The agent prompt tells the agent to write that file; it does not exist for a real user.

3. **What is left is ordinary Claude Code behaviour.** Excluding restarts and agent-notes.md, only five reminders arrived within a running process. state.md (1,994 characters, rewritten by the `state` helpers) and methodology-note.md (1,765 characters) carry 3,759 characters together; the reminders for brief.md, findings.md and methodology.md were empty. The helpers rewriting state.md and draft files is how the release is meant to work. The reminder and the size of its snippet are decided by Claude Code, not by the release.

The agent also blamed someone else in its own feedback: "(harness, not workbench)".
verdicts.narrowed: On a normal interactive host, when a helper rewrites a file the agent has read (state.md, a draft such as methodology-note.md), Claude Code shows its usual file-changed reminder once. In this run that came to about 3.8k characters across 38 minutes. This is standard host behaviour, not a release defect. The repeated, near-whole-file reminders came from the relay restarting the session process every turn and from the study's agent-notes.md file.

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding says the notifications can't be seen in the logs. That is wrong. They are missing from the stream-json relay logs, but Claude Code's own session transcript records them as `edited_text_file` attachments: ~/.claude/projects/-private-tmp-<uid>--<user>-developer-work-analytics-workbench-f40cf0de-cc32-48d4-8475-2335690c867b-scratchpad-sims-retail-B-project/ebd9398b-6924-4c3b-ab8a-63483f4849a2.jsonl. That transcript holds 32 "changed on disk since you last read it" reminders. Sorted by what changed each file:

- **state.md, changed by release helpers (7 reminders, about 33 KB).** This is the only file in Claude Code's tracked set that a helper rewrote. Line 416 comes right after `awb.py state issues --add` and re-shows the whole file, lines 1-24 (2.0 KB). The reminders at later turn starts re-show 30-31 lines, which is the whole file again (5.3-6.1 KB each). The release causes this chain:
  - awb-scope/SKILL.md line 57 tells the agent to "Adapt the brief, state, and history ... populate them with settled facts". The agent did that with the Write tool in turn 2, so Claude Code began tracking state.md.
  - state.md is helper-owned. The template says the table is rendered from findings.json. AGENTS.md line 48 routes changes to findings, issues and next steps through `state finding`, `state issues` and `state next`. run.py also rewrites the file. Every rewrite updates `Last updated` on line 3 and sections lower down, so the diff snippet covers essentially the whole small file.
  - A real user on interactive Claude Code would get the same reminder after each helper rewrite. The in-turn reminder at line 416 shows this happens mid-turn, not only on resume.
- **feedback/agent-notes.md, the harness's own friction log (7 reminders, about 52 KB).** This is the largest share. The agent appended to it with `cat >>` itself.
- **methodology-note.md, findings.md, methodology.md and brief.md.** These came from the agent's own Bash edits (python string-replace scripts and `sed -i`) after it had written the files, not from helpers. export writes only START-HERE.md, manifest.json, charts and datasets (awb_draft.py `_write_text` call sites). findings.md, methodology.md and brief.md reminders carried empty snippets ("changes are not shown here").
- **Repeats at turn starts are a relay artifact.** The relay runs each turn as a fresh `claude -p --resume` (relay.py lines 147-150). Some reminders repeat verbatim: state.md at 416 and 450 have hash 612ac860, and methodology-note.md at 1158, 1322 and 1420 have hash b68ec9ec. An interactive session would not repeat these.

The agent's own note blamed the host ("harness, not workbench"). The finding's framing — whole files re-shown whenever helpers rewrote files it had read — is accurate only for state.md. The release causes that part, and it reaches real users, though it is minor.
verdicts.release_evidence:
- **Instruction to hand-write the file:** awb-scope/SKILL.md line 57 says "Adapt the [brief], [state], and [history] ... populate them with settled facts". The agent did this with Write, so Claude Code tracks state.md.
- **Helpers own and rewrite the file:**
  - awb-init/assets/workbench/AGENTS.md line 48: "Change findings, issues, and next steps with `awb.py state finding`, `state issues`, and `state next`".
  - The state.md template: "The table is rendered from `findings.json`; change it only through `run.py` and `python3 src/awb.py state` commands".
  - awb-init/references/provenance.md: the writer replaces the state file "with `Last updated` set to the local time to the second". Line 3 therefore changes on every write.
  - state.md is written by awb_cli.py and the investigation's run.py.
- **No rewrite of narrative files:** awb-package/assets/awb_draft.py export writes only START-HERE.md (via `_write_start_here`), manifest.json, charts and datasets. It never touches findings.md or methodology.md.
- **No guidance either way:** nothing in the release tells the agent to create state.md by copying the template and filling it only through helpers, and nothing warns about re-reads.
- **Run evidence:** session transcript ebd9398b-....jsonl.
  - Line 416, right after `awb.py state issues --add`: an `edited_text_file` reminder for state.md whose snippet is the whole file, lines 1-24.
  - Lines 721, 819, 1161, 1325 and 1423: whole-file re-shows of 5.3-6.1 KB.
  - The other 25 reminders cover agent-notes.md (harness log) and files the agent changed with its own sed or python edits.
verdicts.narrowed:
Only investigations/<slug>/state.md is affected. awb-scope tells the agent to adapt state.md by hand, which it does with the Write tool. After that, run.py and `awb.py state finding/issues/next` rewrite the whole file, and `Last updated` on line 3 changes every time. Claude Code then attaches a "changed on disk" reminder after each helper rewrite that re-shows essentially the whole 24-31-line file (2-6 KB). Interactive users would hit this too, at a minor token cost. The bulk of what retail-B reported came from elsewhere:
- **Harness friction log:** agent-notes.md, about 52 KB of reminders.
- **The agent's own edits:** `sed -i` and python edits to methodology-note.md, findings.md, methodology.md and brief.md.
- **Relay resume:** each turn runs as a fresh `claude -p --resume`, which repeats already-shown diffs at turn start.

None of those three is caused by the release.

skeptics.corrected_claim: The claim stands as written. I reproduced the numbers and checked each alternative explanation. None of them accounts for the drop as well as the release change does.

Numbers: running kit/reviewloop.py (without --reports) gives these recorded reviews:
- taxi-B: 2 + 2 = 4.
- co2-B: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
- retail-B: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5.
Each run has exactly one full review, its first, and every later review is scoped. No turn records more than two reviews. The agent-008 and agent-007 rows that show "starts=1 (?)" are feedback turns with no record and no reviewer launch. The review-reports folders hold 4, 5 and 5 reports with matching last lines. proposed-issues.md:60 confirms that taxi-B's reply 5 ran 15 of its 21 full reviews on Oct 16.

Metric definition: the Oct 16 figures (21/38/15) were reviewer subagent launches counted by kit/measure.py. I ran that same Oct 16 script on the new B runs and it reports 4, 5 and 5 reviewer subagent runs, so the before and after figures use the same measure. On Oct 16, data.json says no agent tried a scoped re-review, so calling those counts "full reviews" was accurate.

Model and CLI drift: both studies used claude-opus-5-5 on Claude Code 2.1.301 for the agent and codex-cli 0.159.3 for the user. The new rollouts run gpt-6.1-sol, and setup.sh's model line did not change between kits. Roles were the same: in B, Codex played the user and Claude the agent (sim.json codex_role=human).

Harness: I diffed docs/ux-simulation-2026-10-16/kit against the current kit. Personas and human-rules.md are identical. The other changes are:
- path redaction in the docs copy;
- the pinned Sim Analyst git identity, set as an environment variable and as a new "Identity" section in claude-agent-system.md;
- the .ts line timestamps in relay.py;

Mechanism: the release text now says a passed scoped review completes a request. It also says "When a second review in one request still reports problems, stop repairing and start no third review in that request unless the user asks." The runs follow this exactly. taxi-B's reply 5 tells the user "The review rules say I take this to you rather than repairing on a third pass."

User path: the Oct 16 loop happened inside the drafting reply, before any user correction. The new users also asked for corrections, which led to further scoped reviews.

Noise: there are three runs per cell, but all three fell 3x to 8x. All three show the exact full-then-scoped, stop-at-two pattern, and the Codex-agent cells changed only modestly (4/4/6 to 3/3/4). Noise cannot plausibly produce that.

- co2-B agent-004, 7 left;

I checked every number in the claim against the primary sources and they hold.

- taxi-A: agent-007 ran a full review (3 narrative problems, passed=False), then a scoped review (clean, passed). agent-008 ran one scoped review (clean). That is 3 reviews. The main rollout shows 3 spawn_agent calls (12:11:07, 12:14:16, 12:17:28), each inside the right turn.

- So: one full review per run, at most two reviews in any request, and the second review passed in all three two-review turns. That matches the cap in awb-package/references/review.md: "When a second review in one request still reports problems ... start no third review".
- reviewloop.py does report reviewers=0 for the Codex runs.

The Oct 16 baseline matches its README: taxi-A 4, retail-A 4, co2-A 6. Data.json backs the details: co2-A snapshots 001-004 fall inside one turn (A4), and retail-A's four full reviews include a release re-review of an unchanged candidate.

Caveats that make the claim less precise but do not contradict it:
1. **retail-A started a review 5 times but ran 4.** Its agent-007 ran the scoped start twice, the second time after an export refresh and before the reviewer launched. Counted by recorded reviews and reviewer spawns, the total is 4, as claimed.
2. **retail-A did not improve on total reviews.** It went from 4 to 4. It also still ran a review at release, because adding two review rules at release made the receipt stale. The gain there is only that full reviews became scoped ones.
3. **Half the reviews were not fresh reviewers.** 5 of the 10 reviewers were started with fork_turns "all", so they inherited the writer's whole conversation: all three in co2-A and the first two in retail-A. That includes the passing second reviews in co2-A and retail-A. This goes against review.md's "Start a fresh subagent". Oct 16 had the same pattern (retail-A all forked, co2-A mixed), so it does not explain the difference between the studies. It does weaken "every second review passed" as a sign the gate worked.
4. **The Oct 16 baseline cannot be re-derived here.** Its relay logs were not copied. Its own data is loose: the relay showed 5 reviewer launches for taxi-A against 4 snapshot folders, a referee counted 4 reviewer rollouts for co2-A against 6 by snapshots, and an Oct 16 skeptic wrote that the A runs "settled in 2-5 reviews per run".
5. **"Not looping on Oct 16 either" understates co2-A a little.** It ran four full reviews in a single drafting turn, which the new two-per-request cap now prevents. This is mild evidence the fix works in an A run too, though Oct 16 itself called the A loops short.

It still ran a review at release, because adding review rules at release made the receipt stale. Half the reviews (all of co2-A's and retail-A's first two) were full-history forks of the writing agent rather than fresh reviewers, the same pattern as Oct 16. skeptics.reasoning:
The counts hold, and the A runs were not looping on either day. My confound check found only one explanation other than the release, and it accounts for half of the largest drop.

1. **The counts hold on one shared method.** The raw Oct 16 runs survive at <scratch> In both studies I counted reviewer passes inside the Codex subagent rollouts, taking a reused thread's repeated passes into account. Oct 16 gives 4, 6 and 4, all full. Oct 17 gives 3, 3 and 4, with one full review per run and the rest scoped. These match reviewloop.py's receipt records and the spawned threads. So the switch from counting snapshots on Oct 16 to counting receipts on Oct 17 does not change the result. One caution: reviewloop.py cannot measure Oct 16 at all, because review-receipt did not exist in that release. Its starts and records are zero for every Oct 16 run.

2. **Harness, versions and roles are ruled out.**
   - Both days ran codex-cli 0.159.3 with gpt-6.1-sol at high effort.
   - The personas, human-rules.md and referee.md are identical across studies.
   - The kit changed in four ways, none of which touch the Codex review loop: path placeholders, the pinned agent Git identity, relay .ts timestamps, and an identity note in the Claude-agent prompt.
   - Roles were the same (Codex as agent), and every run took the same path: draft, then corrections, then release.

3. **Where the 14-to-10 drop comes from:**
   - **The release turn (product change).** In taxi-A and co2-A the release turn ran no review, because awb-release/SKILL.md:20 now says a current receipt needs no review. On Oct 16 each of those runs had a mandatory full review here. That saves one review per run.
   - **Retail-A (no change).** It ran 4 reviews on both days, including a review at release time on both days.
   - **Co2-A's drafting turn (mainly agent behaviour).** It fell from 4 to 2 mostly because of something the agent did, not the convergence fix. On Oct 16 the agent ran its first `check-draft` only after a clean review (19:53). That pass flagged number conversions and a causal phrase, the repairs went to the reused reviewer, and two more full reviews followed. On Oct 17 the agent ran `check-draft` before the first review (11:44 and 11:45), found nothing, and finished with full then scoped. Both releases say `check-draft` runs last, after the review. Neither requires the Oct 17 order, so the order is agent variance. The new two-review cap would not have stopped the Oct 16 pattern either. Its second review passed, and edits after that would still need another scoped review.

4. **"Every second review passed" is partly built in.** A scoped review judges only changed lines and the prior report's problems. The first full reviews found about the same number of problems on both days: 2, 1 and 3 on Oct 16, and 3, 1 and 3 on Oct 17. So the drafts were no cleaner at first review. The fall comes from narrower re-reviews and the release no longer re-reviewing, not from drafts settling sooner.

5. **There is one run per cell,** so run-to-run noise cannot be estimated. The only drop larger than one review, co2-A's 6 to 3, is the one that agent behaviour partly explains.

The claim's last sentence already concedes that the B runs carry the evidence, which fits these findings.

Each Oct 17 run had exactly one full review, at most two reviews per request, and a passing second review every time, so the two-review cap never triggered. Two changes come straight from the release. First, a release turn with a current receipt ran no review, which saved one review each in taxi-A and co2-A. It also dropped the "JFK trips mostly show the flat fare" clause instead of recording a check, which the agent showed was possible when it did so in agent-006. Both of the next scoped review's problems came from the narrowing. 3 of the 4 problems in the following turn's first review came from the flat-fare wording the user then asked to restore.

skeptics.reasoning:
The core observation holds in all three runs. For the two co2 runs, the release change explains it better than any confound. For taxi-B it does not, and the "regression" label is partly a product of measuring differently.

What holds up:
- **co2-A.** The full review (co2-A/review-reports/agent-006-record01.txt) quotes the new #85 rule: tolerances only in methodology.md or a slide's Notes. The donor note's "emissions totals consistent within source rounding" was supported: eu27-audit has a passing values check, and the 0.02 Mt tolerance was set in [parameters] before the result. The agent's notes say it "Replaced it with a plain statement of EU-check coverage". The Oct 16 rule (git 1db6084, review.md:22) required the note to give the check "with its tolerance", so this deletion could not have happened on Oct 16.
- **co2-B.** The record01 flag rests on the new ban on a tolerance found only in a judgment's `detail`. The agent's own feedback (co2-B/feedback/agent.md, pain point 1) names that rule, says rewording drew new problems, and says it ended up "deleting useful context". The referee says the same. No harness change, CLI drift or persona difference can produce reviewer flags that quote rule text which did not exist on Oct 16. The direction of the agents' behaviour also follows the rule: on Oct 16 they invented tolerances, now they delete. That points at the release, not model drift.

What weakens the claim:
1. **taxi-B is not a side effect of the tolerance fix.** No tolerance is involved.
   - The code-0 narrowing answered the refusal of an exploration query as a citation. That rule already existed on Oct 16: review.md accepted only a result ID or evidence path, and Oct 16 C-07 records such a refusal. The new release added a DQ-plus-scan route, which the agent did not use.
   - The JFK flat-fare line was flagged on two grounds. One is old (no matching claim in methodology.md). The other is #85's new rule on how a source builds a series, which is the C-11 part of #85, not C-10.
   - The agent chose to delete. It kept "meter's time-and-distance fare", now backed by the dictionary, and dropped the true flat-fare remark. The Oct 16 taxi-B Claude agent also trimmed approved lines during review repairs (C-15). So for taxi-B, agent repair style plus older rules explain the deletion about as well as the release does.
2. **"Set up its next two review rounds" overstates.**
   - agent-005-record02 was caused by the code-0 narrowing; the reviewer says so explicitly.
   - agent-006-record01 came from the user's turn-6 base-fare correction. The Oct 16 taxi-B user made the same catch (C-11: "a base-fare definition that left out flat fares"). That is a persona-consistent catch aimed at the definition, which existed before the deletion, so the deletion contributed to that round at most.
3. **The metric changed between studies.** Per-round review reports were extracted only in this study: kit/reviewloop.py says it was "Added 2026-10-17" and writes review-reports/. Oct 16 counted reviews but did not trace what each repair did, and with 15 to 38 reviews per run, deletions could have gone unrecorded. Oct 16 already logged repairs that rewrote approved text (C-15) and spread misleading labels (C-33). So the tolerance-driven route is new, but the general class "repairs damage true content" is not shown to be new.
4. **The co2 losses are narrower than "deleted".**
   - co2-A's statement is still in the deck's speaker notes (released findings.md:118, "consistent within source rounding") and in methodology.md. That is where the Oct 16 proposal for #85 meant tolerances to go. Only the note lost it.
   - co2-B's "recorded check" was a metrics judgment whose detail carried a 1 Mt tolerance chosen after the fact and cited exploration SQL. The new rule itself rejects such a tolerance, so the relabel reflects a conflict in the rules and a split between reviewers, not simply a careless repair. That is still a product cause.
5. **Sample size.** Each instance comes from a single run (3 of 6 runs), so the study cannot say how often this happens.

Whether the general pattern is new since Oct 16 is not shown: only this study extracted per-round review reports, and Oct 16 already recorded review repairs rewriting or trimming approved text (C-15, C-33).

claims.claim: Adding a review rule makes the review receipt stale. The 'ask before repairing' order also caused friction: co2-B's agent repaired first and offered the rule afterwards, and retail-A's agent asked mid-reply and then edited without waiting for an answer.
