claims.evidence: SIMS/co2-B/review-reports/agent-006-record01.txt; SIMS/retail-A/review-reports/agent-009-record01.txt; findings co2-B-06, co2-B-22, retail-A-07, retail-B-10

skeptics.reasoning:
The facts and numbers hold up. Calling this a "regression", and blaming the stale receipt alone, does not.

Confirmed from primary sources:
- co2-B agent-006 (the release turn). The user's message asks to keep the energy-mix distinction as a rule. The agent ran `review-rules add`, then read `review-receipt`, which returned `status: stale` with `changed: ["foundation/review-rules.md"]` and nothing else. It then ran a scoped start (0.33 min, .ts line 17) and a record (0.88 min, line 47), so 0.55 min. The review was clean (agent-006-record01.txt). The whole turn took 1.4 min.
- retail-A agent-009. The user wrote "yes, check later drafts for this too, for all packages". The agent added two rules. The receipt again showed `stale` with only `foundation/review-rules.md` changed. Scoped start completed at 0.46 min and record at 0.87 min, so 0.41 min. A real reviewer subagent ran: Codex rollout 01a149cd, 12:19:55 to 12:20:07, with three tool calls. The report was clean.
- In the other four runs, no release-time review was caused only by a rule. retail-B's release review followed a citation edit. taxi-A recorded its rule in a packaging turn that needed a review for its edits anyway.
- co2-B agent-005 made the energy-mix fix, then ended with "Optional: should future drafts also be checked ... I made the correction in this draft but haven't added it as a rule." The user's message there said "Please finish the corrections and checks".
- retail-A agent-008 asked at 0.3 min with three options and a SKILL quote, said "I'll complete the requested edits either way", and then edited. The instruction is real: review.md:45 says "ask the user before repairing ... Only on their yes, record the rule before repairing".

Where the claim is weakened:
1. **"Regression" is wrong against the Oct 16 baseline.** The Oct 16 reference has no review receipt (zero mentions in README, data.json and proposed-issues). There, `awb-release` "runs a fresh full review even on a draft a clean review just passed" (README:80, C-01; proposed-issues:53/79). Oct 16's own fix proposal (proposed-issues:82) specified a receipt "keyed by a hash of the narratives and the rules file". So a stale receipt after a rule change is the intended #84 design; co2-B-06's tag_reason says "by design". Release-time review cost went down: from a mandatory full review at every release to none in 4 of 6 runs, and a 25–33 second scoped review in 2.
2. **The cause is incomplete.** The extra release review happened because the rule arrived at release. It arrived then because neither agent waited for an answer to the "ask before repairing" question. Had they waited, the rule would have been recorded before the packaging-turn review, and no release review would have been needed. The claim's two halves are one causal chain, not two separate defects. The tradeoff is an extra user round trip against a short scoped review.
3. **The references are partly off.**
   - The staleness comes from #84, the receipt that fixed C-01. Only the "ask first" order comes from #85, the C-06 fix.
   - "Verified C-24" is Oct 16's double-rounding item, which has nothing to do with this.
   - retail-B-10, cited as evidence, is about rule scoping, not staleness or ask-first.
4. **User impact differs between the runs.** The co2-B user did complain that adding a rule "immediately before delivery could trigger another review" (human.md:12, :25). The retail-A user never mentioned the release review; their pain point 7 is about how the question was worded. The retail-A agent listed "Adding rules correctly invalidated the prior review" under what worked well, although it also called the bookkeeping substantial.
skeptics.corrected_claim: New side effect of #84 and #85, not a regression. Adding a review rule makes the review receipt stale by design: the #84 receipt records foundation/review-rules.md, as Oct 16's own proposal specified. This happened in 2 of 6 runs. In co2-B and retail-A the user approved a rule in the release message, so each release turn ran one scoped review whose receipt was stale only because of foundation/review-rules.md. From review-receipt start to record took 0.55 min (co2-B) and 0.41 min (retail-A), and both reviews were clean. Oct 16 instead ran a fresh full review at every release. Both rules landed at release because neither agent waited for an answer to #85's "ask before repairing" question. co2-B's agent fixed the energy-mix wording first, after the user asked it to finish, and offered the rule as optional at the end of its reply. retail-A's Codex agent asked mid-reply with three unexplained options and a skill quote, said it would edit either way, and edited. Had either agent waited, the rule would have been recorded before the packaging-turn review, and no release-time review would have been needed. The co2-B user noticed and disliked the extra review. The retail-A user objected only to the unexplained question.

skeptics.reasoning:
The core facts check out. In co2-B agent-006 and retail-A agent-009, the receipt read returned status "stale" with `changed: ["foundation/review-rules.md"]` and nothing else. In both runs the previous scoped receipt was clean, and the only new event was the user's rule approval. The extra scoped review times are measured from review-receipt start to record: 0.33 to 0.88 min in co2-B, and 27.7 to 52.2 s in retail-A from the raw relay .ts stamps. Model drift does not explain it: co2-B's agent was Claude and retail-A's was Codex. The release text causes it. review.md:39 lists review-rules.md among the receipt inputs, and review.md:45 and SKILL.md:24 require asking before repairing.

Several confounds and framing problems weaken the claim:

1. **The two halves are one chain, and they depend on the agent's choice and the user's path.** Each extra review happened only because the agent had already repaired before the user said yes. The user's yes then arrived alone, in the release message.
   - co2-B: the user wrote "Please finish the corrections and checks". The agent made the energy-mix fix and offered the rule afterwards (agent-005.out.md).
   - retail-A: the user wrote "If they look right, I'll mark it delivered". The agent posted the question and said "I'll complete the requested edits either way".
   - In the other runs, the rule was added in the same turn as the repairs, and the receipt diff also listed findings.md and methodology.md, so one review covered both. taxi-A's user volunteered the rule; taxi-B and retail-B answered while asking for more corrections. co2-A added no rule.
   - So this happened in 2 of 6 runs. An agent that followed the ask-first order would have paid an extra user round trip instead of an extra review.
2. **Harness.** retail-A's "asked mid-reply" placement is partly a relay artifact. The relay's `_codex_reply` joins every interim agent_message into one reply, and the Oct 16 study already scored this as a harness effect: C-44 says codex exec renders the question tool as text. Not waiting was still Codex's deliberate choice.
3. **"Regression" holds by construction, not by measurement.** The review-receipt and release gate came in with #84 (cf9a0d5), which is not an ancestor of the Oct 16 base 1db6084. Oct 16 therefore has no baseline for this metric. Oct 16 also already had release-time reviews (co2-A ran one at release). The staleness comes from #84's fingerprint; #85 (6da2956) added the user's yes. Blaming #85 alone is imprecise. The receipt behaviour is by design: findings.json tags it so, and the retail-A agent called the invalidation "correct".
4. **Who felt the friction.** The ordering friction was reported by the agents. co2-B-22 is agent-sourced only. The retail-A user's complaint was about three unexplained options and a quoted skill line, not about the order. Only the co2-B user flagged the extra review. Each review took about half a minute and needed no user decision.
5. **Metric definitions differ.** co2-B-06 cites reviewloop's "review tail" of 1.0 min, measured to the end of the turn, while the claim uses 0.55 min from start to record.
6. **One citation does not fit.** retail-B-10 is about scoping rules to an investigation and supports neither the staleness point nor the ordering point.
skeptics.corrected_claim:
This release stales the review receipt whenever foundation/review-rules.md changes. That is by design: #84's receipt covers the rules file, and #85 adds a rule only after the user says yes. As a result, a rule approved in the same message as the release request forces a scoped review at release. This happened in 2 of 6 runs, once with each agent model:
- co2-B (Claude agent): 0.55 min from review start to record.
- retail-A (Codex agent): 0.41 min.

- co2-B: the user asked it to finish, so the agent repaired first and offered the rule afterwards.
- retail-A: the agent posted the question as an interim message, which the relay joined into the middle of its reply, and made the edits without waiting.

In taxi-A, taxi-B and retail-B, the rule was approved together with further corrections, and one review covered both. Neither extra review needed a user decision.

The ask-before-repairing order conflicts with a correction the user has already authorised. Both agents reported this. The retail-A user objected to the question's unexplained options rather than to its timing. There is no Oct 16 baseline, because the receipt did not exist on 1db6084.

Every count holds when re-derived from the parent Codex rollouts. The overstated parts are what the forked reviewers actually inherited and who observed it.

Counts. I read the spawn_agent calls in each parent rollout under agent-home/.codex/sessions/2026/10/17/:
- co2-A (rollout ...07-17-59-01a14995-3b8a): package_review at 11:45:39, package_review_scoped at 11:46:47 and precision_review at 11:52:55. All three used fork_turns 'all'.
- retail-A (rollout ...07-17-58-01a14995-3812): package_review at 12:11:53 and package_review_scoped at 12:13:46 used 'all'. Both ran in the full-draft turn (12:06:25 to 12:15:05, ending "eight-slide draft ... ready"). wording_review at 12:17:58 ran in the corrections turn and release_rule_review at 12:19:55 in the release turn; both used 'none'.
- taxi-A: board_draft_review, board_draft_review_scoped and delivery_corrections_review all used 'none'.
- No exec input contains a nested spawn_agent, followup_task or send_message call, so these are all the reviewers.
- The child rollouts agree. The 'all' children carry forked_from_id and subagent_history_start_ordinal. The 'none' children have a single session_meta and a single user message.

Rule and baseline.
- review.md line 7 says "Start a fresh subagent, so the agent that wrote the draft does not review it", and line 11 repeats it for Codex.
- Codex's own tool text calls fork_turns 'all' a "full-history fork", so calling the forked reviewers not fresh is fair.
- Oct 16 C-59 is final 'contested' in data.json. Its harness verdict recorded the same agent-dependent pattern: retail-A forked all four reviewers, taxi-A used 'none' and co2-A used both. So "still depends on the agent" holds.

Overstatement 1: "inherited the writer's whole conversation."

- Token counts show this. At spawn the parent's input context was 280,631, 288,510 and 331,724 tokens in co2-A, and 120,534 and 127,981 in retail-A. The forked children's first calls used 21,914, 21,878 and 22,580 tokens (co2-A) and 25,325 and 25,308 (retail-A). Unforked children started at 17,573 to 17,737. So forking added only about 4k to 8k tokens.
- retail-A's parent had compacted at 12:02:43, nine minutes before the spawns. Its forked reviewers got the earlier user messages verbatim, an encrypted compaction summary, the last agent reply and the current request, not the conversation verbatim.
- What was inherited can still bias a reviewer. co2-A's precision_review opened with the writer's "Independent review and final package checks passed" and the user's "This is strong."

Overstatement 2: "observed by the referees."
- This is true only of the comparison workflow's review-loop referees. Their journal entries 37 and 63 name fork_turns 'all' for co2-A and retail-A.
- The per-run simulation referees did not observe it. retail-A's orchestrator-report.md line 72 says "The agent's notes confirm a fresh read-only reviewer for each round". co2-A's report and taxi-A-26 say the spawns are not visible in the relay logs, and taxi-A-26 says reviewer isolation "cannot be audited".

skeptics.reasoning:
The counts are exact, and no confound I tested explains the behaviour. Two parts of the claim's framing do not hold.

**Counts.** I read the spawn_agent calls in each A run's main rollout under agent-home/.codex/sessions/2026/10/17/.
- co2-A: package_review, package_review_scoped and precision_review were all spawned with fork_turns "all". Each child's session_meta has forked_from_id, and each child holds all 8 or 9 of the writer's user messages.
- retail-A: package_review and package_review_scoped, in the drafting turn after the 12:06 headline message, used "all". wording_review (12:17) and release_rule_review (12:19) used "none".
- taxi-A: all three spawns used "none". Those children have no forked_from_id and start from AGENTS.md.

**Confounds tested.**
- CLI or model drift: none. All three A runs ran codex-cli 0.159.3 with gpt-6.1-sol at high reasoning effort, and their config.toml files are identical apart from paths. Oct 16's data.json names the same CLI and model.
- Persona, path or harness: these vary between runs, but retail-A switched from "all" to "none" inside one session, on the same release, harness and persona. Nothing visible prompted the switch. That rules out every run-level confound, so model discretion is the best explanation.
- Compaction: does not explain it. taxi-A compacted before its "none" spawns, co2-A did not compact before its "all" spawns, and retail-A compacted before its "all" spawns.
- Cross-study pattern: it looks like noise. On Oct 16 retail-A used "all" four times, taxi-A used "none", and co2-A used both. Now co2-A is all "all" and retail-A is mixed. Only taxi-A was stable (both times "none"); two observations cannot separate a persona effect from chance.
- Release change: the Codex sentence in review.md ("start a fresh subagent all the same") is the same in the Oct 16 release (commit 5808614) and in this one. No release text mentions fork_turns, so "unchanged" is accurate and there is no product change to confuse with noise.
- Metric definition: both studies read fork_turns from the same rollout files.

**Where the framing fails.**
1. "Against review.md's fresh-subagent rule" overstates it. review.md never says what "fresh" means in Codex terms. Codex's role prompt presents fork_turns as "how much context you want to propagate", and full history is what you get when it is omitted. co2-A's agent called its full-history fork "A fresh reviewer" (main rollout line 720), so it apparently believed it was following the rule. The cause is the release's undefined term meeting Codex's full-history default, not an agent defying a clear rule. Oct 16's skeptic made the same point.
2. "Observed by the referees" is not supported. The per-run referee reports (feedback/orchestrator-report.md and findings.json) never mention fork_turns. taxi-A's referee wrote that reviewer isolation "cannot be audited" from the event stream, and the co2-A and retail-A referees note that the relay log leaves spawns out. The observation comes from the agent-home rollouts, not from the referees.
3. Minor: retail-A's forked reviewers inherited a compacted history, meaning every prior user message, an encrypted summary and the current turn. That is the writer's conversation in compacted form, not the raw transcript.

skeptics.reasoning:
The timing numbers hold, apart from one rounding slip. The claim's framing does not hold.

**How I checked.** I re-ran kit/reviewloop.py, read-only (without --reports), on all six runs. I also recomputed each draft turn from the .err start stamp and the .ts line stamps, up to the first non-help `review-receipt start`.
- **Turn lengths match the user waits:** co2-A agent-006 10.41 min, taxi-A agent-007 14.70, taxi-B agent-005 13.40, co2-B agent-004 10.19, retail-B agent-005 11.67. These agree with the transcript times, for example taxi-B 11:40:32 to 11:53:56 and retail-B 11:36:34 to 11:48:14.
- **Minutes before the first review start:** co2-A 7.29 ("about 7" is fine), taxi-A 10.40, taxi-B 7.16 (the claim says 7.1; it rounds to 7.2), co2-B 5.04, retail-B 5.52. retail-A was left out of the claim but is consistent: agent-007 had 5.35 of 8.69 min before its first review.

**Problems:**

1. **"Most" is true only for the Codex-agent (A) runs.** The share of the draft turn spent before the first review was co2-A 70%, taxi-A 71% and retail-A 62%. The Claude-agent (B) runs were taxi-B 53%, co2-B 49% and retail-B 47%, so two of the five cited runs are under half by the claim's own numbers. Summed over the five draft turns it is 35.4 of 59.4 min (60%). Across all B-run requests that had a review, the time from the first review start to turn end is the larger part: taxi-B 10.8 of 19.4 min, co2-B 9.75 of 16.2, retail-B 10.65 of 18.2 (56-60%).

2. **"Still" reverses the Oct 16 reference it cites.** Oct 16 C-08 in the README says: "Most packaging time still went to the review loop, not to reading." C-01 and its skeptic agreed. So this run shows a shift, caused by the review loop now being capped. It is not a pattern that carried over.

3. **The retail-A example is not an instruction read.** The "manifest of about 20k tokens" is the draft's own generated `manifest.json`. It was read with `cat` in correction turn agent-008 (20,088 tokens against a 1,400-token output budget). The agent called that read "my poor choice" (agent.md line 82; agent-notes line 128). retail-A's real instruction truncations were batched skill and contract reads of 19,979 and 10,479 tokens in preview turn agent-006 (agent-notes line 110).

4. **The co2-B figure is the agent's own estimate, and the logs bear it out.** In agent-004 the template reads were 2,944 + 22,283 characters and review.md was 14,893, about 10k tokens. agent-003 also read package-contract.md (20,569 characters). The numbers check out. In this re-run, relay/state.json conversation_minutes are 62.6 for taxi-A, 39.2 for co2-A and 63.5 for retail-A, a mean of 55.1. - **Metric definition:** the metric is computed the same way in both studies, from relay start to the user's DONE line (relay.py `conv_min`). The kit diff against docs/ux-simulation-2026-10-16/kit shows only three changes: a per-line .ts timestamp pump, the SIM_GIT identity env for the agent, and path placeholders.
- **Personas and rules:** personas, human-rules.md and referee.md are identical.
- **CLI and model versions:** both studies ran codex-cli 0.159.3 and Claude Code 2.1.301. The Codex agent is gpt-6.1-sol at high effort in both, and the Claude user is claude-opus-5-5 in both.
- **The user role's own time:** human turns took about 2-3 minutes in every run of both studies, so nearly all wall-clock is Codex agent time.

The claim's figures are accurate, but two confounds weaken how the claim reads.

1. **The user took a different path in each run, and work volume moved with wall-clock.** User messages rose from 9/7/8 to 10/9/10. Retail-A's user asked for extra deliverables this time: a review of non-product codes before lock-in, and a second Q4 ranking restricted to products cancelled by at least 3 customers. The user also picked a £1,000 threshold, where the Oct 16 user picked £10,000. I counted Codex sampling steps and output tokens from the parent rollouts. Retail-A went from 90 to 132 steps and from 119k to 175k output tokens (+47%), against +29% wall-clock. Co2-A went from 115 to 100 steps and from 126k to 112k tokens (-11%), against -22% wall-clock. Taxi-A went from 144k to 162k tokens (+12%), against +5% wall-clock. So the per-run up and down pattern follows persona choices and path, and nothing ties it to the release.

2. **Codex was uniformly faster on Oct 17.** I timed steps under 60 seconds. They took 2.42, 2.31 and 2.43 seconds per 100 output tokens on Oct 16, and 2.09, 1.98 and 2.07 on Oct 17. That is about 14% faster, with nearly the same gain in every run. At matched output sizes, time-to-first-item was lower in 7 of 9 bins. The runs started at different times of day: 19:17Z on Oct 16 and 11:17Z on Oct 17. The B runs also finished in 31-43 minutes this time, against 75-143 on Oct 16, so the A runs shared the machine less near their ends. Because the effect is uniform across runs, an environmental cause fits it better than the product.

Taken together, total parent output across the three A runs rose about 15% (389k to 449k tokens), and the faster backend absorbed most of that. Flat wall-clock therefore does not show that the release left Codex-agent time cost unchanged. At Oct 16 speed, the mean would plausibly have been around 60 minutes or more. That figure is an estimate, not a measurement.

There is also one run per dataset, with no replicate to estimate noise. Per-run swings of 11-14 minutes are within what the path differences above produce.

The headline figures (49.4 to 63.5, 13 to 17.5, and 12.2, 17.5 and 6.3 for replies 3 to 5) are exact. The 41-minute split, the "settled" wording and the regression framing need qualifying.

The numbers hold up. I checked them three ways. kit/measure.py is byte-identical to the Oct 16 copy in docs/ux-simulation-2026-10-16/kit. state.json's conversation_minutes uses the same relay-start-to-DONE definition as Oct 16's 49.4. 1. **The user took a different path.** Both runs used the same persona file (kit/personas is identical), but the Claude-played user asked for different things. On Oct 16 there were 8 messages and 7 replies; now there are 10 and 9. Both extra stops came from the user.

   - Message 5: "I'll decide which version goes in the deck once I've seen both". That forced reply 5 (Q4 version B plus status, 6.3 min).
   - Message 4 asked for a with/without sensitivity check of all five answers. Its sensitivity queries and producers are inside reply 4. Reply 4 also spent about 2 min on charts and a report file that nobody asked for (the agent's own choice).
   - On Oct 16 the user said "Go ahead and bring the data in once scope is settled". The agent then did intake, all five analyses and the headline preview in one 11.8-min turn, with no stop.

2. **The longer single wait is partly turns merging.** On Oct 16 the agent reported "5 answered" before showing numbers (C-04), so the user spent a whole exchange getting the tables: reply 3, 9.5 min. Those answers took 11.8 + 9.5 min over two turns. Now the answers and tables arrive in one 17.5-min turn, which is what the C-04 fix intends. The longest wait rising from 13 to 17.5 min does not show that answering takes longer overall.

3. **The packaging split mixes definitions.** On Oct 16, measure.py counted reply 2 (intake, analysis and headline preview) as packaging: 33 of 47 min, leaving 14 outside. The claim's 41 drops agent-001 from packaging, although measure.py flags it.

   - Comparing 41 with the Oct 16 table's implied 14 makes the shift look nearly twice as big as it is.

4. **One run per cell, and the A runs did not move together.** The Oct 16 README says "One run per cell" (not three). In this re-run, taxi-A moved +3.1 min (59.5 to 62.6) and co2-A moved -11.2 (50.4 to 39.2). The A-run mean barely changed (53.1 to 55.1). Retail-A's +14 min is not a trend across the variant.

Both days used the same Codex model setting (gpt-6.1-sol in setup.sh), and Codex CLI 0.159.3 was in use both days. Replies 3 to 5 had no backend errors. Oct 16's 13.3-min longest wait was itself slowed by three 403 reconnects.

6. **The release still contributes.** The release now under test is 1677d19 (verified against the release folder). It makes cross-sheet "copies" an explicit user decision (awb-clean). It also adds analysis work: reconcile() on every filtered population, period-coverage counts, proposing thresholds before results, and showing evidence before calling questions answered. These add minutes and would have forced an intake stop even without the user's request. But the old release text also left repeated rows to the user, and the Oct 16 agent decided the overlap itself, so some of the difference is agent behaviour. Several of these costs are intended fixes for C-19 and C-04, not plain regressions.

With n=1 and a visibly different user path, the release's share of the extra ~14 min cannot be separated out.

Its 0.02 Mt basis appears only in the builder-only methodology.md. co2-B's reviewer refused the "within 1 Mt" bound, which the agent had chosen after seeing a 0.913 Mt gap and recorded only in a judgment detail. The agent cited a source reference rather than inventing a pre-recorded tolerance, at the cost of deleting useful context (co2-B-02, major). On Oct 16, co2-B invented a 0.15 Mt tolerance after a 0.13 Mt gap and shipped it in the note and slide notes. taxi-A shipped "zero-record tolerance" on a visible appendix slide.

skeptics.reasoning:
Confounds do not explain the shift as well as the release change does. What breaks is the claim's universal wording and part of its metric.

Why the product explanation holds:
- The persona folders are byte-identical to the Oct 16 kit (diff -rq printed nothing).
- human-rules.md, referee.md and skill-list.md are unchanged. claude-agent-system.md differs only in its Python path and the added Git identity block. No harness file mentions tolerances.
- Role assignment is the same in both studies: A runs have Codex as the agent and B runs have Claude (sim.json `codex_role`). Oct 16 co2-B also had Claude as the agent.
- The mechanism is visible in the logs:
  - co2-A's reviewer cites the new rule verbatim ("permit tolerance statements only in methodology.md or a slide's Notes").
  - co2-B's reviewer cites it too ("a tolerance only in a judgment detail, not in brief or [parameters]").
  - The released text uses the "exactly" wording that the new templates prescribe.
- Model or CLI drift and noise cannot be excluded. On counts alone, 0 of 6 against 2 of 6 is not significant (Fisher p ≈ 0.45). The reviewer-text evidence is what ties the change to the release.

Where the claim overstates:
1. **"No tolerance reached any released audience text" is false as written.** co2-A's released findings.md carries the phrase the first review classified as a tolerance:
   - line 70 Notes: "emissions totals agree within source rounding"
   - line 118 Notes: "consistent within source rounding"
   The release's own package-contract.md:11 calls findings.md the "audience-facing deck outline". The first review caught the phrase only in methodology-note.md:27, and the reviewer explicitly let it stand in slide Notes. It is release-compliant, because it is backed by `[parameters].eu27_rounding_tolerance_mt = 0.02`, which methodology.md:47 cites.
2. **The metric differs between studies.** Oct 16 C-10 counted co2-B's 0.15 Mt in speaker notes (released line 144) as well as in the methods note. Getting "none" this time requires leaving speaker notes out. Also, co2-A's 0.02 parameter was written after an exploration query (agent-003 line 41) had already shown differences of about 0.001 Mt, though the value was derived from a rounding bound.
3. **co2-B did not avoid writing a tolerance after seeing the data.** The agent wrote "within 1 Mt over 1850-2024" into a judgment detail (settings.toml:68) after exploring. It never reached audience text: the review refused it instead of demanding one. So "refused rather than invented" describes the review's behaviour, not the agent's. The refusal also cost the run useful context (co2-B-02, major: 4 of 9 and 4 of 7 review problems were about reconciliation wording). The orchestrator also filed co2-A's catch as friction (co2-A-20), not as a win.

claims.claim: Methods-note length now follows the brief. All six briefs record about 500 words, and the released methodology-note.md files run 488-569 words by wc -w. On Oct 16, taxi-B shipped an 867-word note against a one-page request.
claims.evidence: wc -w of SIMS/*/storage/releases/*/*/001/methodology-note.md (521, 566, 502, 543, 488, 569)

skeptics.reasoning:
The numbers for this run check out. The comparison with Oct 16 does not.

What holds:
- `wc -w` on the six released notes in storage gives taxi-A 521, taxi-B 566, co2-A 502, co2-B 543, retail-A 488 and retail-B 569, exactly as stated. Each storage copy is byte-identical to `project/deliveries/*/*/released/001/methodology-note.md`.
- All six `investigations/*/brief.md` files have the line "Methods note length: about 500 words" (taxi-A:29, taxi-B:39, co2-A:27, co2-B:33, retail-A:45, retail-B:29).
- The users asked for "one page" in every run. The brief template (`awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/brief.md:19`) turns that into "about 500".
- check-draft in this release has a new informational `note_length` row. It fires when a note runs more than 10% over the length the brief records (`awb_draft.py` around line 2873; CHANGELOG line 54). I ran each project's installed `note_length_problems` read-only on the released notes. It counts 512, 542, 495, 523, 481 and 543 words and raises no rows.
- The relay logs show the check at work. It flagged drafts at taxi-B 562, co2-B 556 and retail-B 590 words. It also flagged retail-A's brief line, which was not written in the required form. The agents trimmed or fixed each one (the co2-B agent wrote "an overlong methods note"). No user had to ask for a shorter note.

What fails:
- The Oct 16 contrast is wrong. Oct 16 taxi-B did not ship an 867-word note. The Oct 16 `data.json` C-70 verdicts say its first note was 770 words and grew to 867 over 15 reviews. Reply 5 called it "a one-page methodology note". The user then asked for about 500 words in message 6. The agent added R-methodology-note-001, and the released note is 506 words.
- The Oct 16 README says the same twice: line 322 reads "taxi-B's released note 506 words", and line 97 says the reviews passed a note that "grew from 770 to 867 words during those reviews".
- So the shipped length on Oct 16 already roughly matched the request. The real change is how that happened: the user caught it on Oct 16, and this time the automatic check did.
- Only two Oct 16 runs stated a length at all: taxi-A wrote about 400 words, and taxi-B released 506 after the user stepped in. The other Oct 16 drafts ran 635 to 884 words, but their users never asked for a page length. "Length now follows the brief" therefore describes a change in process, not in what was shipped, for the one comparable case.

Minor points:
- By `wc -w`, taxi-B (566) and retail-B (569) run 13-14% over 500. They pass only under check-draft's own count, which leaves out Markdown syntax.
- co2-A's user feedback cites a 489-word note. The released file is 502 by `wc -w` and 495 by the tool's count. This does not change the result.
skeptics.corrected_claim: The methods note now holds to the recorded length without the user stepping in. All six briefs record "Methods note length: about 500 words". The new check-draft note_length row flagged over-length drafts in taxi-B (562), co2-B (556) and retail-B (590), and the agents trimmed them before release. No user had to ask for a shorter note. On Oct 16, taxi-B's draft grew from 770 to 867 words across 15 reviews that passed it, and the agent reported it as "one-page". The user had to ask for about 500 words, and the released note was 506 words.

skeptics.reasoning:
The product change is real, and the logs show it working. The claim's comparison with Oct 16 is still mis-stated, and part of what it reports comes from a change in what the users asked for.

What holds:
- The release added a `Methods note length: about <n> words` line to the brief template, noting that one page is about 500 words, and an informational `note_length` row in check-draft (awb_draft.py:2873-2913; helpers.md:35).
- The relay logs show this check causing the result. In all three runs where Claude was the agent, the first check-draft flagged the note: taxi-B at 562 words, co2-B at 556 and retail-B at 590, each against 500. The agent then trimmed it, and every later check-draft returned an empty `note_length`.
- No user in this re-run complained about note length (grep of all six transcripts).
- In retail-A, the check flagged a brief line written in the wrong form and the agent rewrote it.
- The persona files, human-rules.md, relay.py, referee.md, setup.sh and claude-agent-system.md are identical to the Oct 16 kit on every line about length. Harness drift does not explain the result.
- I found no Oct 16 model or CLI version record, so model drift cannot be ruled out. But the trims follow the check in the logs, which a model change would not explain.

What is wrong or confounded:
1. **The Oct 16 figure is a draft, not a release.** "taxi-B shipped an 867-word note" is false. 867 words was the draft after 15 reviews. The user then asked for about 500 words, and the released note was 506 (Oct 16 data.json C-70). This study measures released notes, so the comparison sets released notes against a peak draft. Comparing releases, taxi-B went from 506 to 566 by `wc -w` (542 by the release's own counter). Oct 16 taxi-A, a Codex run that asked for one page, released 399 words. So Oct 16 also shipped notes near one page. The real difference is that Oct 16 needed the user to correct it, and the first drafts were much longer: Claude's taxi-B first draft was 770 words on Oct 16 and about 588 now.
2. **The user path changed.** The personas are unchanged, and co2 and retail ask only for "a methodology note". On Oct 16 those four users asked for a "short" note or none. This time all four asked for one page, and that is why all six briefs record 500. The reason may be the new README sentence ('A methods note length, such as "one page"...'), which is part of the product, or persona variance. Either way, the Oct 16 co2 and retail notes (drafts of 635 to 884 words) had no recorded length to break, so they are no baseline for "follows the brief". In a real run where the user never states a length, the template still says "a page or two".
3. **The `wc -w` figures can fail the claim's own test.** taxi-B at 566 and retail-B at 569 are 13 to 14% over "about 500", beyond the release's 10% band. They pass only by the release's counter, which gives 542 and 543.
4. **Small sample.** There is one run per cell. Only one Oct 16 run (Claude taxi-B) is a true case of a note breaking a stated length, and Codex taxi-A already met it on Oct 16.

The direct log evidence keeps the product explanation stronger than any confound. But the stated baseline is wrong, and the "all six" framing depends on a change in what users asked for.

claims.claim: There are still no defaults for showing numbers to a given audience. co2-A's semi-technical donor draft carried 8,645.2 Mt and 23.57%, which cost a full correction round of 6.7 min. taxi-A's lay board deck defaulted to 24-hour times until the user asked for 12-hour ones.
claims.oct16_ref: #85 / Oct 16 C-33 (display-precision part); verified C-07 (partly fixed)
claims.evidence: SIMS/co2-A/feedback/human.md item 1; SIMS/co2-A/relay/agent-007.jsonl; findings co2-A-01 and taxi-A-07

skeptics.reasoning:
The primary sources back the main facts:
- co2-A's first message calls the donors "semi-technical: they read charts well but don't want jargon". The draft findings.md, as agent-007 read it at the start of its turn, says "annual CO2 rose by 8,645.2 million tonnes in China" and "US 23.57%, EU-27 16.27%, China 15.46% and India 3.58%". foundation/display.toml set [round] change_mt = 1 and world_share_percent = 2.
- agent-007.ts runs from 1792237744.4 to 1792238146.9, which is 402.5 s, or 6.7 min. The orchestrator report gives the same span: 11:49:04 to 11:55:47.
- taxi-A's brief calls the audience a "Non-technical Lab board". The draft read in agent-008 has "Both months peak at 18:00" and "25.63% at 08:00 to 28.21% at 18:00". The user asked for 12-hour times in msg 8 (human-008.out.md item 2).
- In the release, the brief template records a precision only "when the user states them". awb-package sets [round] to "the places the slide's number format shows". Nothing sets a default by audience, and nothing tells the agent to ask. So "no defaults" holds.

Five problems weaken the claim:
1. **"Unchanged" overstates.** Commit 5896cfe (#85, Oct 16 22:52) shipped after the Oct 16 study. The brief template's Audience section now offers a precision line that later packages reuse. review.md now flags "a number shown with more decimal places than a precision the brief's Audience states". The display-precision part of Oct 16 C-33 is therefore partly addressed for a precision the user states. What remains is that there is no default and no prompt to ask. In co2-A the brief held no precision until agent-007 wrote one, so the new check had nothing to enforce.
2. **The 6.7 min turn was not only about precision.** The same request also removed stray full stops from the slide 5 and slide 6 headlines; the orchestrator labels the turn "Rounding and punctuation edits". Much of the turn was overhead that any correction triggers: check-draft passes, an export retry, and a scoped review starting about 223 s in. About 33 s (121 s to 154 s in) went to a workaround that belongs to co2-A-02: a new recorded result, territorial-change-tonnes, so that check-draft would accept "about 8.6 billion tonnes". The user had dictated that wording; a default would not have produced it. The orchestrator itself puts the remaining cost in this workaround. Precision was the main content of the round, but not the whole of it.
3. **The unit is quoted wrongly.** The slide text says "8,645.2 million tonnes". The "+8,645.2 Mt" form appears only in the headline preview and the internal methodology.
4. **taxi-A's time format did not cost a round of its own.** The 12-hour request was one of three corrections in msg 8. That message also asked for awb-status and the release, and the whole exchange took about 3.3 min (12:15:44 to 12:19:04). The finding is rated minor.
5. **The cross-reference "verified C-07 (partly fixed)" does not check out.** Oct 16 C-07 is "Standard reconciliation checks are not set up with results", which has nothing to do with display precision. I found no other list where C-07 means this.

That turn was mostly rounding, but it also removed two headline full stops, and part of its time went to a check-draft workaround (co2-A-02, a new recorded result so the "about 8.6 billion tonnes" wording would trace). taxi-A's draft for a non-technical board used 24-hour times (18:00) until the user asked for 12-hour times, as one of three corrections in msg 8.

skeptics.reasoning:
The core of the claim holds, and it comes from the release text, not the harness. The brief template (awb-init/assets/workbench/investigation/brief.md:19) records a precision only "when the user states them". awb-package/SKILL.md:30 asks about the audience only when it is missing and records a precision only if the user states one. review.md step 3 flags only "a number shown with more decimal places than a precision the brief's Audience states". 1. **"Unchanged" is wrong about the release.** Since Oct 16 the release records a precision the user states, and the review checks numbers against it. That is #85 fix item 4, implemented as written. What remains is narrower: there is no default when the user names only an audience. The defect persists in a narrowed form; it is not unchanged.

2. **The agent model explains the symptoms about as well as the release does.** Both cited cases come from Codex-agent runs. Where Claude was the agent, it chose audience-friendly formats unasked:

It also included a scoped review. Not all 6.7 min was spent on precision.
   - taxi-A's 12-hour request was one of three corrections in message 8 and cost no round of its own.

claims.claim: The review's closed readability list still lets technical prose and typos through. taxi-A's released findings.md has '27.65% at 6-7 p.m..' on the tipping slide, and jargon-heavy files went to users for review in taxi-A and retail-A.
claims.evidence: SIMS/taxi-A/storage/releases/trip-pattern-comparison/board-brief/001/findings.md; findings taxi-A-23 and taxi-A-08

skeptics.reasoning:

(1) The typo is real. In taxi-A's released findings.md, line 60 on the tipping slide reads "25.37% at 8–9 a.m. to 27.65% at 6–7 p.m..". The claim writes a hyphen where the file has an en dash, which is trivial. The claim also undercounts. Line 23 on the volume slide has "Both months peak at 6 p.m..", and the released methodology.md line 61 ends "6 p.m. and 7 p.m..".
(2) All of these came from the agent's own 12-hour regex (.workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py) in turn agent-008, after the full review in agent-007. "27.65% at 6" appears only in agent-008.jsonl. agent-007 shows "27.65% | 18:00, 19:00".
(3) The only review that saw this text was the scoped review in agent-008. Its Codex reviewer rollout (agent-home/.codex/sessions/.../rollout-2026-10-17T08-17-28-01a149cb...jsonl) ran nl -ba and sed -n '37,160p' over findings.md, so it read the lines. It returned only "R-time-format-001 pass ... review (scoped): clean". reviewloop.py shows no review in the release turn (agent-009 starts=0).
(4) That matches the release design. review.md step 3 says "readability, only these": glossary terms, precision above the audience's stated level, record words or IDs, and imperatives. Step 4 says "Report exactly this, and nothing else". Typos and general technical wording are outside the list. So "the closed list lets typos through" is supported.

Where the claim overreaches:
(a) The jargon evidence it cites for taxi-A, taxi-A-08, is quality-proposal.md. The user was handed that file in reply 3 ("ready for review"), and it does carry Q-011, publication.json, canonical view and fare_amount. But it is an awb-clean intake document, not a package draft. The package review never reads it, and the finding's own tag_reason blames the clean skill's templates. It is a separate gap and says nothing about the review's readability list. Better taxi-A evidence exists but is not cited: 24-hour times passed review (taxi-A-07), and the reviewer pushed an internal QA bullet onto the tipping slide (taxi-A-03).
(b) No retail-A finding supports "jargon-heavy files". retail-A-06 is about jargon in chat (commit hashes, check counts), not files. The primary sources do show technical prose surviving the review. The draft that passed agent-007's full and scoped reviews contained "grouping keys", "signed quantity" and "permitted repeated line occurrences", none of them glossary terms. The user asked for plain English in msg 8. But the user rated it "Minor: some jargon remains in notes" and called the files "good overall" and "solid" (human/notes.md Turn 8; feedback/human.md section 6). "Jargon-heavy" overstates it.
(c) "Still lets typos through" implies a carry-over, but Oct 16 C-33 covered wording, definitions and precision, not typos.
(d) The cross-reference "verified C-50" does not match Oct 16's C-50, which is about START-HERE listing files as both attach and internal. It looks like a mis-citation unless it refers to another list.
skeptics.corrected_claim: The package review's readability check is a closed list: glossary terms, precision, record words or IDs, and imperatives, then "report nothing else". So typos and general technical wording are never checked. In taxi-A turn 8, the agent's 12-hour time conversion left double periods in the released findings.md: "6 p.m.." on the volume slide and "27.65% at 6–7 p.m.." on the tipping slide, plus one in methodology.md. A fresh scoped reviewer read those lines and reported clean. In retail-A, the deck draft passed full and scoped review while still carrying "signed quantity", "grouping keys" and "permitted repeated line occurrences". The user had to ask for plain English, calling it a minor issue in an otherwise good draft. taxi-A's jargon-filled quality-proposal.md (taxi-A-08) did go to the user for review, but it is an awb-clean intake document outside the package review: a separate gap, not evidence about the review's list.

skeptics.reasoning:
The claim's structural core holds, and no harness confound touches it. The readability item at release awb-package/references/review.md:28 is closed by design. It says "readability, only these" and lists four things: a glossary term used without its definition, precision finer than a precision the brief's Audience states, record words or IDs, and imperatives. Typos and general technical wording are not on the list. Oct 16 proposed-issues.md:165 (#85) asked for exactly this "narrow readability item". That is a property of the release text, not a behavioural measurement. The cited evidence, though, is weaker than the claim implies:

1. taxi-A-08 is misattributed. The jargon-heavy file was quality-proposal.md, an awb-clean output at the cleaning step (turn 4; taxi-A/feedback/human.md item 6, human/notes.md:23). Package review never reads it: per review.md:18 the review reads findings.md, methodology.md and the note. So this finding says nothing about the review's readability list; it belongs to a separate clean-skill finding. The taxi-A user did not report jargon in findings.md itself; their complaint there was that it was long and hard to picture as slides.

2. The double period comes from the user's path and the agent's method. It is not evidence that the problem persists. The draft had no "p.m.." until turn 8. The user asked late for 12-hour times. The Codex agent then ran .workbench-tmp/revise_board_delivery.py, a regex that rewrote "HH:00" to "N a.m./p.m.". Where the original sentence ended "18:00." this produced "6 p.m.." on two lines (findings.md:23 and :60, not just the tipping slide). After that only a scoped review ran. Its receipt reads "R-time-format-001 pass ... review (scoped): clean", and awb-release accepted the scoped receipt. The reviewer did read the changed lines and behaved exactly as specified, since typos are out of scope. Oct 16 C-33 has no typo baseline (its examples are undefined terms, precision, arrows and imperatives), so "still" is a new category, not a persisting one. No other run's released findings.md has a double period.

3. The remaining support is in scope and real. In retail-A, the draft's notes and methodology note carried non-glossary terms ("signed quantity", "grouping keys", "permitted repeated line occurrences"). They passed review, and the user asked for plain English (retail-A human/notes.md:63). The cited retail-A finding (retail-A-06), however, is chat jargon, which is also outside the review. Stronger support the claim does not cite: co2-A-01 (too much precision, while the brief stated no precision, so the closed list could not fire) and taxi-A-07 (24-hour times for a lay board).

4. Role confound, which is weak. Both cited runs are variant A: Codex agent, Codex reviewer subagent, Claude user. There are three runs per cell. Oct 16 C-33 spanned both agent models, though, and B-run users (Codex) also requested wording fixes, so persona sensitivity alone does not explain the pattern. The relay, git identity and CLI versions have no plausible bearing on draft wording.

Net: the mechanism (a closed list) is real and by design. The typo instance comes from one path, the taxi-A jargon instance is outside the review's scope, and the label "unchanged from C-33" overstates persistence. 1. **The cited lines are wrong.** Q-011 asks whether to leave rate-code-99 credit-card trips out of the tip figures. It was open only from reply 3 (11:35:54Z) until user message 4 (11:36:11Z). Both come after the decision. At both times every ledger question was answered, so "0 open" was correct. The pending item at line 479 was a review wording choice about code 0, which is not a ledger question. The only status line written while Q-011 was open is line 212 (reply 3). The finding taxi-B-11 and orchestrator-report row 7 both point to reply 3 ("A3"), not to lines 401 or 479.

It also leaves out that the same line names the pending decision as the next step. The decision was left out of the count, but the line did not hide it.

The defect is in the template's design: it counts root questions only and leaves open child decisions out of the count. That still confused the user. human.md says "the agent reported no open questions while asking me to decide the tipping population", and human/notes.md turn 4 says the same. Reply 1 says "before I create the investigation", and brief.md was created at 11:20:54Z, after reply 1 at 11:20:00Z. agent.md section 2 and agent-notes.md turn 1 both say the agent improvised. But the improvised line, "Your five questions: none recorded yet · next: your answers to the four decisions above.", was accurate and drew no complaint from the user.

There is one real taxi-B instance, but it sits at the wrong line, it is a different defect from Oct 16 C-04, and run-to-run variance explains whether it shows up at all. The co2-B half is not evidence that the line is unreliable.

1. **Wrong lines cited.** The Q-011 case is taxi-B reply 3, transcript line 212: "5 answered (provisional), 0 open". At that point the ledger in commit 412d7d9 shows Q-011 (a must-answer decision for the user, under Q-003) as open, and the agent's own tool output in relay/agent-003.jsonl says "Q-011 open". By lines 401 and 479 the user had already settled Q-011 in message 4. What was pending there was headline approval, the data-file choice and the code-0 wording. Those are package decisions, not ledger questions, so "0 open" was accurate at both lines and each line's "next:" named the pending item.

Its "next:" clause named the pending rate-code decision, and a "Decision for you" section sat directly above it. This run's agent dropped the decision count. Whether pending sub-decisions appear in the line therefore depends on what the agent volunteers, and with one run per cell that is noise. The wording is inconsistent, but none of these lines is false.

skeptics.reasoning:
The facts in the claim are accurate. In co2-B/transcript.md, reply 2 says "Earlier years count as zero in the cumulative totals" and reply 3 says "I also calculated a ceiling". User messages 3 and 4 challenge both, and human.md ranks this as pain point 1. What does not hold up is the label "unchanged", along with "mishandled for the third study in a row". The main reason is that the metric was redefined between studies.

In that run the gap first appeared in A5, using the reviewer's "count as zero" wording. This time the agent flagged the gap on its own in the first answer (A2), which is what the released #87 guidance asks for (analysis.md line 15; awb-explore/SKILL.md line 52):
   - Its Q4 query computed years_with_data.
   - It recorded DQ-004 in quality.md: "China's CO2 series starts in 1907 and India's in 1858 … Cumulative sums since 1850 treat missing early years as zero, a small understatement for China and India".
   - It attached that as a caveat on the q4 finding (relay/agent-002.jsonl).
   
   Measured by Oct 16's definition, C-20 did not happen again. To call it unchanged, the claim has to quietly widen the metric from "gap not flagged" to "gap worded badly".

2. **The errors were in wording, not in the numbers.** The released methodology.md lists both corrections under "Methodological corrections" and says "values did not change" both times.
   - Summing only the reported years treats missing years as zero. "Count as zero" describes that arithmetic correctly. The recorded caveat already called the result an understatement; the chat summary left that out. The user's own notes object to the missing qualifier ("could mislead donors unless qualified"). The agent then conceded more than it needed to.
   - The "ceiling" bullet stated its assumption right next to it ("That assumes early emissions were no higher than in the first reported year").

The persona brief and human-rules.md do not prompt it about missing data, so the challenge was genuine. But a different persona could reasonably have accepted both wordings.

3. **The error is different each study, and milder each time.**
   - Oct 15: the agent asserted the early years "matter little".
   - Oct 16: the gap was not flagged until A5. "Count as zero" came from the reviewer. The correction then claimed without support that OWID's World series also omits those years.
   - Now: the gap was flagged at A2. The correction cites OWID's processing code, so it is supported. Only the "ceiling" framing went too far.
   
   Calling all three one unchanged defect hides this trend.

**Confounds I ruled out:**
- The harness (relay timestamps, git identity, disclosure prompts) has no plausible effect on what A2 said.
- The role assignment was the same as Oct 16: Claude played the agent and Codex played the user.
- The task structurally guarantees the gap. That holds across studies, so it does not explain why the wording recurred.
- The Claude model version used on Oct 16 is not recorded in the reference material, so I could not test model drift. It is a minor uncertainty.

**A smaller inaccuracy in the finding:** co2-B-01's tag_reason says the guidance "gives no prompt to state how missing years enter a cumulative sum". In fact the agent stated exactly that, prompted by the new guidance. The defect is in how it was worded, not in whether it was disclosed.

**Net:** a pattern genuinely recurred: in every study the user had to correct how the missing years were described. But it should be rated partly fixed, not unchanged, and "major" probably overstates a wording problem that never changed a number.
